title: Jev studied 438,122 apps doing $10k/mo+ for me. The bar is stupidly low
body:
i know you've seen everyone's agents build mobile apps on X.

literally every day, someone posts: “launched on iOS app store in 24h" then two weeks later: “i hit $4k MRR” and the replies are always the same:

> “what did you build it with?” “how did you get users?” “drop the sauce”

after seeing enough of these, you eventually start wondering:

> “should i be building mobile apps too?”

short answer: F*CK YEAH.

especially if you’ve spent the last few years building SaaS.

and especially if you’ve convinced yourself consumer apps aren’t for you because you’re a “b2b person.”

because there’s a decent chance you’ve already spent years selling to consumers. you just happened to put a SaaS dashboard in front of them.

here’s why i think that distinction matters, and exactly how i’d go from nothing to a mobile app worth publishing as quickly as possible.

# you might already be doing b2c

there’s a pretty standard piece of startup advice that gets repeated everywhere:

- sell to businesses

- businesses have money

- b2b customers stick around longer

- consumers don’t want to pay

sounds reasonable.

until your “b2b SaaS” is a $19/month analytics tool sold to solo founders.

you didn’t escape b2c.

you just picked one of the hardest groups of consumers imaginable.

indie hackers and small founders are incredibly price-sensitive. they understand how software works, they compare everything, and they’ll happily spend three hours looking for an open-source alternative to avoid paying you $20/month.

and half of them are thinking:

> “i could probably build this myself.”

putting a Stripe subscription on something doesn’t magically make it b2b.

the more useful distinction is why somebody buys.

a company usually buys software because there’s an economic reason to do it. it saves employees time, reduces costs, increases revenue, replaces another tool or makes some process easier.

consumers buy for a completely different set of reasons.

they want to sleep better.

look better.

save more money.

stop wasting time.

get stronger.

eat better.

feel more organized.

learn something.

quit something.

feel less anxious.

become more confident.

or simply feel like they’re making progress.

and these problems are enormous because basically everyone has them.

you also don’t need to convince a procurement department, integrate into somebody’s 14-tool stack or explain ROI on a sales call.

you need to make one person look at your product and think:

> “wait, i want this.”

that’s a very different playground.

and right now, mobile apps are one of the easiest ways to play in it.

# why mobile is suddenly interesting again

a few things are happening at exactly the same time.

1. ai has destroyed a huge part of the technical barrier

building a decent mobile app used to mean learning Swift or Kotlin, understanding a completely different ecosystem, fighting Xcode, figuring out app architecture and probably spending months before you had something worth showing people.

that’s changing extremely quickly.

a focused consumer app can now go from an idea in your head to something usable in a day.

the bottleneck is increasingly not:

> “can i build this?”

it’s:

> “should i build this?”

which is a much more interesting problem.

2. consumer distribution is everywhere

TikTok, Reels and Shorts can put a completely unknown product in front of millions of people without that company having an existing audience.

you don’t necessarily need SEO.

you don’t necessarily need paid ads.

you don’t necessarily need 50,000 Twitter followers.

one good piece of content can create the first few hundred or thousand users you need to figure out whether there’s something there.

3. mobile fits perfectly into that distribution

see video.

understand problem.

download app.

try product.

that entire journey can happen in a few minutes, on the same device.

there’s almost no context switching.

4. you can test ideas insanely fast

this might be the biggest change.

if building an MVP takes three months, choosing the idea feels incredibly important.

if building an MVP takes a day or two, the economics completely change.

you don’t need to discover the idea.

you need to find something interesting enough to test, build the smallest version that proves the core behavior, put it in front of people and see what happens.

if nobody cares, you learned something.

if people use it once but never come back, you learned something else.

if 100 people download it and 25 are still opening it a week later, now things get interesting.

so here’s exactly how i’d approach it.

# FIRST STEP

## 1) find demand before finding an idea

don’t open a blank Notion page and brainstorm “startup ideas.”

you’ll probably come up with solutions to problems that exist mostly inside your own head.

instead, start by watching people.

for consumer products, one of the best places to do that is TikTok.

download it.

spend 5–10 mins/day intentionally looking for patterns.

not random viral videos. human behavior.

look for:

- things people constantly complain about

- habits they’re trying to quit

- things they’re insecure about

- things they flex about

- things they obsessively track

- new aesthetics and identities

- challenges everyone suddenly starts doing

- things people wish they were better at

- routines people keep sharing

- things people repeatedly ask for help with

- behaviors that already require some annoying workaround

you’re basically looking for human problems hiding underneath trends.

for example:

there’s a trend called “underconsumption core.”

the surface-level trend is people buying less stuff.

the obvious founder-brain reaction would be:

> “let’s build an underconsumption app.”

don’t.

instead, ask why millions of people relate to it.

maybe the actual problems are:

> “i impulse-buy when i’m stressed.”

> “i keep buying stuff i don’t need.”

> “saving money feels boring.”

> “i have no idea where my money disappears every month.”

> “i want to feel rewarded for not buying something.”

those are much more interesting.

now you can start imagining actual product loops.

maybe every time you resist buying something, you add it to the app and your “money saved” counter increases.

maybe you photograph something you’re about to buy and the app makes you wait 24 hours.

maybe friends compete over who avoided the most unnecessary purchases this month.

the trend gave you the signal.

the underlying behavior gives you the product.

the 3 consumer app formats i keep coming back to

you don’t need to invent some completely new category either.

most interesting consumer apps fit into a few basic structures.

tracker

turn invisible behavior into numbers.

spending. screen time. sleep. habits. mood. food. focus. workouts. sobriety. reading. studying.

people love seeing themselves quantified because something abstract suddenly becomes progress they can see.

“i’ve been focusing more lately” is vague.

“my average focus time went from 41 minutes to 76 minutes” feels real.

coach

help somebody become a slightly different version of themselves.

daily missions. challenges. plans. reminders. personalized recommendations. feedback.

people often don’t need another complicated tool with 40 buttons.

they need something that understands their goal and tells them:

> “do this next.”

the product becomes valuable because it removes decisions.

simple utility

take one annoying thing and make it pleasant.

timers. lists. journals. notes. widgets. planners. calculators. scanners.

the functionality can be ridiculously simple if the experience feels good enough.

a product doesn’t need 25 features to deserve a place on somebody’s home screen.

sometimes one feature used every day is much stronger.

steal ideas from the comments

one more trick:

when you find a trend, search the comments for words like “app.”

people literally write:

> “someone needs to make an app for this”

or:

> “is there an app that does this?”

or:

> “i wish something tracked this automatically.”

that’s basically free product research.

and it’s much more useful than asking people:

> “would you use an app that does X?”

because they’re already expressing the problem without you putting the idea in their head.

## 2) define the loop before you build anything

before touching code, answer one simple question:

what does somebody repeatedly do inside this app?

not what features does it have.

what’s the loop?

for a spending app it might be:

> almost buy something → log it → resist purchase → see money saved → feel progress → repeat

for a fitness app:

> open app → receive today’s workout → complete it → see progress → come back tomorrow

for a focus app:

> choose task → start timer → finish session → build streak → repeat

if you can’t explain the core loop in one sentence, the app is probably still too complicated.

then ask yourself four more questions:

what makes someone download it?

there should be a very obvious promise.

what makes someone understand it in 10 seconds?

the value shouldn’t require a tutorial.

what gives them their first win?

get them there as quickly as possible.

what makes them open it tomorrow?

this is the one founders often forget.

downloads are nice.

retention is the product.

you don’t need perfect answers yet. you just need enough clarity that you’re not asking an AI to invent your entire business while it writes the code.

## 3) borrow the patterns, not the pixels

once you have an idea and a basic loop, don’t design everything from scratch.

you’re probably not a product designer.

neither am i.

instead, find 5–10 successful apps around the same problem or user behavior.

they don’t even need to be direct competitors.

if you’re building a savings app, maybe one app has incredible onboarding, another has a great streak system, another has a satisfying progress screen and another has a paywall you like.

download them.

actually use them.

then screenshot everything:

- first launch

- signup

- onboarding

- home screen

- navigation

- core action

- empty states

- progress screens

- streaks

- notifications

- upgrade prompts

- paywall

- settings

the useful part isn’t the colors or rounded corners.

it’s the decisions underneath them.

where do they ask questions?

how many onboarding screens are there?

when do they show the actual product?

when do they ask for notification permissions?

when do they ask for money?

how quickly do you get your first win?

what information is permanently visible?

what gets hidden?

what makes you come back tomorrow?

these companies have already tested thousands of tiny decisions you’d otherwise be guessing about.

so don’t invent every interaction from zero.

study what works, understand why it works, combine the best patterns and add your own touch.

for younger consumer audiences, i generally like:

- one obvious action per screen

- huge typography

- very little text

- visible progress

- streaks

- milestones

- satisfying numbers

- personalization early

- very obvious feedback when something is completed

basically:

make progress impossible to miss.

if somebody completes something, celebrate it.

if they’ve used the app for seven days, show them.

if they improved 18%, show them.

if they saved $143, make that number impossible to ignore.

the user should constantly understand:

> “this is working.”

## 4) turn the references into an actual app

this is where building gets stupidly easy.

i’ve tried most of the tools people use for building software with ai.

but if i want to go from an idea to an actual mobile app quickly, i use Shipper.

at this point you should already have:

- your app idea

- your core user

- the outcome you’re promising

- your main product loop

- screenshots of apps that solve similar problems well

take all of that and give it to ChatGPT, Claude or Grok first.

don’t say:

> “build me a budgeting app.”

you’re giving the model almost nothing to work with.

instead, give it a proper job:

> “i’m building a mobile app that helps {user} achieve {outcome}. study the attached references and break down the ux patterns, visual hierarchy, onboarding, navigation and interactions they use. redesign those patterns around my product. define every mvp screen, what happens on each screen, the full onboarding journey, main navigation, core user loop and one mechanism that gives users a reason to return regularly. remove anything that isn't necessary for the first version. finally, turn everything into a detailed build prompt.”

now you have something much closer to a product spec than a random prompt.

read it.

remove the stupid stuff.

add anything it missed.

then take that output, attach your screenshots and put everything into Shipper.

tell it exactly what you want.

the screens.

the interactions.

the flow.

the logic.

the tiny details.

then keep talking to it like you would a developer sitting next to you:

> “make this screen simpler.”

> “move the paywall after the user gets their first result.”

> “add a 7-day streak here.”

> “this onboarding feels too long. cut it in half.”

> “save this state when the user closes the app.”

> “make this interaction feel more native to iOS.”

> “there are too many choices on this screen. make one action dominant.”

this is where people get AI builders wrong.

you don’t need to know Swift.

you don’t need to manually create every component.

you don’t need to set up a giant dev environment just to find out whether anybody wants your idea.

but you still need taste.

you still need to make decisions.

you’re basically directing the product while Shipper builds it.

and the quality of the result depends heavily on the quality of those decisions.

the biggest difference is how you talk to the ai.

don’t just tell it to “make an app.”

keep forcing it to think about the user:

- what do they see first?

- what do they need to understand here?

- what is the single most important action?

- how quickly do they experience the main benefit?

- where could they get confused?

- what information can we remove?

- what makes this satisfying?

- what gives them a reason to open it tomorrow?

that usually produces something much better than endlessly prompting for new features.

## 5) make the first version good enough to charge for

once the main experience works, stop adding random functionality.

focus on three things.

onboarding

treat onboarding like its own product.

because for most users, it basically is.

they haven’t experienced your product yet. they have no loyalty to you. they can close the app in two seconds and never think about it again.

find good onboarding flows, screenshot them and repeat the same reference process.

your goal is simple:

the user should understand why they downloaded the app and experience value within 30 seconds.

every onboarding screen should earn its existence.

if you ask a question, use the answer.

if you ask for a permission, explain why.

if something can wait until later, move it later.

and if you have eight onboarding screens because every other consumer app has eight onboarding screens, you’re doing it wrong.

then give those references to Shipper and iterate until the whole thing feels obvious.

monetization

once the product works, add your subscription and paywall.

don’t spend three days debating whether your yearly plan should cost $27.99 or $31.99.

you have no data yet.

a perfectly normal place to start might be:

- $4.99/week

- $29.99/year

you can test pricing later.

what matters more initially is when you ask for money.

if possible, let the user understand the value first.

let them create something.

see a result.

finish their first session.

get their first personalized plan.

then put the paywall in the path of continuing that value.

you want the user thinking:

> “i want more of this.”

not:

> “what the hell am i paying for?”

polish

then use the app.

a lot.

don’t stare at the home screen and decide it looks finished.

actually behave like a user.

start from a fresh account.

tap things in weird orders.

deny permissions.

close the app halfway through onboarding.

open it again.

leave fields blank.

use absurd inputs.

come back the next morning.

give it to friends without explaining anything and watch where they get stuck.

you’ll discover an unbelievable number of tiny things that made perfect sense to you because you built it.

every confusing interaction you remove makes the product feel more trustworthy.

and whenever something feels wrong, go back to Shipper and describe exactly what you want changed.

you’re not trying to make the first version perfect.

you’re trying to make sure the core loop feels finished.

## 6) ship before you feel ready

once the main loop works:

# SHIP IT.

don’t spend another month adding social features, achievements, AI assistants, custom themes and 14 settings because you’re scared of publishing.

the first version isn’t supposed to prove you’re a genius.

it’s supposed to answer one question:

does anyone actually want this?

publish it.

make content about the problem.

send people to it.

watch what they do.

read the reviews.

look at where onboarding drops.

look at how many people actually reach the core action.

look at how many come back the next day.

look at how many come back a week later.

look at who pays.

then fix what’s broken and ship again.

personally, i’d start with iOS and only worry about Android once the idea has earned the extra work.

and i’d keep the first version almost painfully focused.

one audience.

one problem.

one promise.

one core loop.

you can always make the app bigger after people care.

making something smaller after you’ve built 30 features is much harder.

the weird thing about building consumer apps right now is that the technical barrier that stopped most of us from doing it has basically disappeared.

you used to spend most of your energy figuring out how to build the thing.

now you can spend much more of it on the parts that actually make the thing work:

finding a real behavior.

turning it into a product people understand immediately.

giving them a reason to come back.

figuring out distribution.

you can figure out what people want on TikTok, study the apps already winning their attention, turn those patterns into a proper product spec and have Shipper build the thing.

then put it in front of real people.

you don’t need to know whether it’s a $10k/mo app before you start.

you just need to get version one into somebody’s hands.

preferably before the 18-hour timer runs out.

title: I manually studied 30,600 iOS apps making $20k-100k/mo+, the recipe is stupidly easy
body:
Only around 1.7% of apps in the iOS App Store make $20k/mo+.

That's still more than 30,000 apps.

I've spent a stupid amount of time studying them manually. No AI summaries, no giant scraped dataset. Just looking at what these apps actually sell, how they onboard users, how they market themselves and why people keep paying.

I've also lost $300k+ making expensive mistakes of my own.

And the annoying part is that most of those mistakes were completely avoidable.

So if you can't afford to spend years and hundreds of thousands of dollars figuring this stuff out yourself, you probably can't afford to ignore what is already working.

Mobile apps are especially interesting right now because the hardest part used to be building them.

You needed Swift. You needed developers. An MVP could take months. Then you still had to somehow get the thing through the App Store.

That's changed.

Claude Code, Shipper and the rest of the AI coding wave have made building dramatically easier.

Which means the advantage moved somewhere else:

Picking the right idea. Shipping fast. Getting people to pay. And DISTRIBUTION.

@chddaniel and I have spent years building internet businesses together, and after studying thousands of successful apps, you start noticing something:

The same patterns show up constantly.

The ideas repeat.

The onboarding repeats.

The marketing repeats.

You don't need to reinvent everything. You need to understand why these patterns work and execute them better.

If I were starting from zero today, here's exactly what I'd do.

## 1. START WITH A PROBLEM PEOPLE ALREADY WANT SOLVED

Your app idea matters way more than most founders want to admit.

You can execute almost everything else correctly and still make the business unnecessarily difficult because you picked a problem nobody cares enough about.

It's called B2C for a reason.

Business to consumer.

Yet somehow the consumer is usually the part people forget.

Before thinking about features, branding, UI or which AI model you're going to use, figure out who is actually supposed to pull out their card and pay for this thing.

Then ask the question that matters more:

Why would they care enough to do it?

If I had limited time and money, I'd heavily favor problems people already feel every day:

- losing weight

- looking better

- screen time addiction

- getting over an ex

- sleeping better

- quitting an addiction

- relationships

- tracking food

- getting stronger

You don't need to educate people about these problems.

They already think about them.

They Google them. They watch TikToks about them. They complain about them to friends.

And, most importantly, they already spend money trying to solve them.

Look at Cal AI.

📷 cal ai website

The entire product can basically be explained in one sentence:

Take a photo of your food and instantly track the calories.

That's it.

Obviously there's more happening inside the app, but the reason someone downloads it is immediately understandable.

People want to lose weight.

Tracking calories helps.

Manually searching for ingredients and entering every meal is annoying.

Cal AI removes that friction.

The app reportedly did around $28k in its first month, $115k in its second month and eventually reached roughly $1m in monthly recurring revenue within six months.

The lesson isn't to open Shipper and build Cal AI #483.

The lesson is that a simple solution attached to a massive existing desire can become an enormous business.

Competition is usually a good thing

A lot of founders see competition and immediately assume they're too late.

I'd often think the opposite.

Steve Hoyek's Journable is a good example.

It entered calorie tracking, one of the most crowded consumer app categories imaginable.

Instead of trying to invent a completely new category, they looked at what people disliked about the existing products.

A lot of calorie trackers had become bloated and complicated.

Journable went in the opposite direction and focused heavily on simplicity.

It eventually crossed $100k/month, with most of that revenue reportedly coming from Android, which is interesting by itself considering how obsessed mobile founders tend to be with iOS.

Competition can be one of the strongest forms of validation you have.

If you find five apps solving roughly the same problem and they're doing $20k, $50k or $100k+ every month, you know people are willing to pay.

Compare that with finding a completely untouched idea.

Maybe you've discovered an incredible blue ocean.

Or maybe nobody built it because nobody wants it.

I'd rather have evidence.

Before committing to an app, I'd want to know:

Are multiple competitors making serious money?

How big did the winners get?

What do customers hate about the existing products?

And probably most importantly, how are those apps acquiring customers?

Because distribution should influence the product you decide to build.

An app that can be understood in a 7-second TikTok demo has a completely different growth profile from something requiring three minutes of explanation.

An app where users naturally share results has an advantage over one where everything happens privately.

A transformation product naturally creates before-and-after content.

These things matter before you write a single prompt.

Don't spend weeks trying to invent a problem nobody has ever solved.

Find a market where people already spend money. Understand why the winners work. Figure out what customers still hate. Then build something meaningfully better, simpler or different.

You don't need to reinvent human behavior.

Build around behavior that already exists.

## 2. VALIDATED THE IDEA? BUILD IT FAST.

Once I've convinced myself the market exists, I want the first version in the App Store as quickly as possible.

Not three months.

I'd aim for 7 days, maybe 14 if the product genuinely needs it.

Every additional week before real users touch the product increases the chance you're building something nobody actually asked for.

Your first version basically needs three things:

1. Onboarding

2. Monetization

3. The core app loop

That's the app.

Everything else can come once actual people are using it.

And this is where building apps in 2026 is completely different.

With Shipper, you don't have to start with an empty project and manually translate everything in your head into code.

But that doesn't mean you should open it and type:

"build me a fitness app"

and expect a great product to magically appear.

📷 shipper website

Research before you prompt

Before building anything, I'd download 5-10 of the best apps in the category.

Actually use them.

Go through the entire experience like a customer.

Screenshot their:

- onboarding

- paywall

- home screen

- core feature

- results

- interesting interactions

Also pay attention to what they don't include.

Then stop looking at the screenshots as designs and start asking why the decisions were made.

Why does onboarding ask that question?

Why is the paywall shown at that exact moment?

Why are there only three actions on the main screen?

Why does the result look like that?

Why did they remove everything else?

You're not trying to clone somebody else's app.

You're reverse engineering the decisions underneath it.

Once you understand those decisions, you can give Shipper dramatically better context.

Instead of describing everything with words, show it.

Give it screenshots.

Give it visual references.

Explain the user journey.

Tell it what happens when somebody opens the app, what their main action is, what happens afterward and how the whole thing should feel.

AI builders are only as good as the context you give them.

If you're vague, you're effectively asking the AI to make dozens of product, UX and design decisions for you.

Then people blame the builder when the result looks generic.

Don't make it guess.

My process would basically be:

#1 Find the apps already winning in your niche.

#2 Break down their onboarding, paywall and core loop.

#3 Decide what yours does differently or better.

#4 Give Shipper the plan, screenshots and visual references.

#5 Build and keep iterating until it feels like something you'd actually download yourself.

That last part matters.

A functioning app isn't a finished app.

If the first version looks generic, keep going.

If the spacing feels wrong, fix it.

If the typography looks cheap, change it.

If a screen has 12 things happening at once, simplify it.

If you can't explain what you want, find an app that does it properly and attach the screenshot.

There's basically no reason anymore for vibe coded to automatically mean AI slop.

The tools are good enough.

You need enough taste to recognize when something isn't finished and enough patience to keep iterating until it is.

For consumer apps, this matters even more because UI itself can become distribution.

Someone sees your app for three seconds in a TikTok and immediately wants to know what it is.

Users screenshot their results and send them to friends.

Your app looks polished enough that creators actually want to show it.

Apple features it.

Design isn't just decoration anymore. It can directly affect acquisition.

So yes:

BUILD FAST.

But fast doesn't mean shipping whatever AI gives you after prompt #1.

Use Shipper to compress months of development into days.

Then use some of the time you saved to make the product actually feel worth paying for.

## 3. THE DOWNLOAD ISN'T THE SALE

This might be the most important section of the entire article.

By the time someone reaches your onboarding, you've already done something difficult.

They saw your TikTok.

Stopped scrolling.

Clicked.

Went to the App Store.

Downloaded the app.

And actually opened it.

You might've paid to acquire that person. Or spent hours making the content that brought them there.

Now you have one job:

Don't waste that attention.

Yet most apps immediately do.

"Welcome!"

"Here are our 3 amazing features!"

"Create your account!"

Nobody cares.

Onboarding shouldn't feel like an instruction manual.

It should feel like they've already started using the product.

📷 Provide a caption (optional)

Think about onboarding as moving someone through a sequence of beliefs:

I have this problem → this app understands my problem → this might actually help me → I want the result

Then you ask them to pay.

That's why every screen needs a reason to exist.

Some questions personalize the experience.

Others force users to think about the severity of their problem.

Some introduce proof.

Others create small commitments before asking for a larger commitment.

And whenever possible, give them a taste of the actual product before the paywall.

Building a calorie app?

Don't use 15 screens to explain how incredible your scanner is.

Let them scan something.

Building a screen-time app?

Show them what their current behavior actually looks like.

Building a looksmaxing app?

Give them part of their analysis.

Ideally, the user reaches your paywall already wanting whatever is on the other side.

Don't invent onboarding from scratch

The biggest apps in your category have spent years testing this.

Questions.

Screen order.

Copy.

Paywalls.

Prices.

Offers.

They've probably tested hundreds of variations you'll never see.

You get to study the result of all those experiments for free.

Again, don't blindly copy the screens.

Understand the patterns.

If three of the largest apps all ask a similar question before revealing the result, pay attention.

If they introduce social proof at roughly the same moment, pay attention.

If everyone delays the paywall until after giving the user something personalized, that's probably worth testing too.

Cal AI shows how far this can go.

Their team reportedly ran 123 A/B experiments, tested 160 unique paywall designs and created 424 total variants, including 61 meaningful experiments specifically around the onboarding paywall.

During that period, monthly revenue grew more than 3x and trial-to-paid conversion improved by 31%.

That isn't one genius onboarding flow somebody designed in an afternoon.

It's hundreds of small decisions being tested until the numbers moved.

That's how I'd treat yours too.

Your first onboarding isn't your onboarding.

It's hypothesis #1.

Get people through it.

See where they disappear.

Change the opening.

Remove unnecessary screens.

Move the aha moment earlier.

Change the questions.

Move social proof.

Test the paywall.

Test the offer.

You don't need to redesign everything every week.

Sometimes moving one screen or changing one sentence affects every single user who downloads the app afterward.

Your onboarding and paywall are never really finished.

They're part of your growth engine.

## 4. START DISTRIBUTION BEFORE THE APP IS FINISHED

Don't wait for App Store approval to start thinking about marketing.

While the app is being built, go back to the competitors you researched earlier.

This time, ignore their product.

Study how they're getting customers.

Find their TikToks and Instagram accounts.

Search their app name and see which creators are posting about them.

Find the founder.

Find their ads.

Save every piece of content that performed unusually well.

At this stage, you're not trying to prove how original you are.

You're trying to understand what the algorithm and the customer have already proven they respond to.

Look at:

the hook,

the first frame,

how quickly the app appears,

how they demonstrate the product,

and the CTA.

If the same format works repeatedly across several apps in the same niche, that's free market research.

Then make your own versions.

A lot of them.

The Marketing Hierarchy

This is how I think about whether marketing is actually working:

Tier 0: Low views

Tier 1: Views

Tier 2: Views + Engagement

Tier 3: Views + Engagement + Downloads

Tier 4: Views + Engagement + Downloads + Conversions

Tier 5: Views + Engagement + Downloads + Conversions + Low churn

The tier you're stuck at tells you what to fix.

At Tier 0, the content isn't working. Nobody stops scrolling. Fix the hook before worrying about anything else.

At Tier 1, you've figured out attention.

That's nice.

But 500k views producing almost no downloads isn't successful marketing just because the number underneath the video looks impressive.

Tier 2 can be even more deceptive.

Thousands of likes. Hundreds of comments. People arguing.

Maybe the creator is entertaining.

Maybe the topic is controversial.

Maybe everybody loves the video.

None of that means they want the app.

Don't celebrate engagement until you've confirmed that engagement moves people further down the funnel.

At Tier 3, the content is finally doing its job.

People watch, understand the product and download it.

If you're getting thousands of downloads but almost nobody pays, stop blaming your videos.

Marketing did its job.

Your problem moved further down the funnel.

Go fix onboarding, the paywall or the product.

Tier 4 is where the pieces connect.

Views become downloads.

Downloads become paying users.

Now you have something worth scaling.

And Tier 5 is the actual goal.

Marketing worked.

Onboarding worked.

People paid.

Then the product delivered enough value that they stayed.

That's why I don't really care about "going viral" by itself.

A video can get 5 million views and make almost nothing.

Another can get 100k views and generate thousands of dollars because almost everyone watching is exactly who the app was built for.

The goal isn't views. The goal is moving people through the entire hierarchy.

When something works, stop trying to be clever

This is one of the easiest mistakes to make.

You finally find a format that works.

You post it five times.

Then you get bored.

So you decide your audience must be bored too and start making something completely different.

But you've seen every single one of your posts.

Your audience hasn't.

If one hook consistently produces downloads, make 20 more versions.

If screen-recording demos work, keep making them.

If slideshows work, make more slideshows.

Change the story.

Change the opening.

Change the person.

Change the example.

Change the visual.

But keep the underlying format that already proved itself.

Volume matters because you're running experiments.

Ten videos tell you almost nothing.

After 50, 100 or 200, patterns become obvious.

Certain hooks constantly outperform.

Certain problems get stronger reactions.

Certain demos produce more downloads.

Certain creators convert dramatically better.

That's when you multiply yourself.

Don't immediately chase influencers with massive audiences.

I'd rather find smaller creators who clearly understand short-form content.

Someone with 8,000 followers and several 500k-view videos might be far more useful than someone with 300,000 followers whose audience barely responds to anything they post.

Look at whether they understand hooks.

Whether they're good on camera.

Whether they communicate well.

Whether they've repeatedly demonstrated that they can stop the scroll.

Then don't ask them to invent your marketing strategy from scratch.

Give them what you've already learned.

Your winning videos.

Competitor examples.

Hooks.

Screen recordings.

Angles that already generated downloads.

You want creators producing more variations of a strategy you're already proving.

That's when distribution starts looking less like random posting and more like a machine.

Instead of you making five videos, five creators make five each.

Then ten creators.

Then more accounts.

Suddenly you're testing hundreds of creatives and learning much faster than someone posting whenever inspiration strikes.

And those organic winners tell you exactly what to do next.

## 5. PUT MONEY BEHIND WHAT ALREADY WORKS

Paid acquisition should come after you've learned what people respond to.

Too many founders reverse this.

They build an app.

Make three random ads.

Put $200/day behind them.

Lose money.

Then conclude that paid acquisition doesn't work.

You just paid to test something you could've tested organically.

If you've already produced 100 pieces of content and five generated most of your downloads, those five concepts are where I'd start.

Keep the underlying ideas and make variations:

different hooks,

different creators,

different openings,

different demos.

Paid ads should amplify something that's working, not rescue something that isn't.

Once you start spending, the business also becomes much easier to understand.

Imagine spending $1,000 and getting 500 installs.

50 start a trial.

20 pay.

Now you can actually see the machine.

Improve the creative and maybe $1,000 buys 700 installs.

Improve App Store conversion and more visitors download.

Improve onboarding and maybe 75 people start trials instead of 50.

Improve the paywall and perhaps 30 pay instead of 20.

Then improve retention and every customer becomes worth more.

That's where things get interesting.

Small improvements start multiplying through the entire funnel.

You're no longer optimizing random screens.

You're improving the economics of the business.

Now improve the product

Only once I had meaningful usage would I start spending significantly more time expanding the product.

Because now you have evidence.

Read App Store reviews.

Read support messages.

Read refund requests and cancellation reasons.

Find where people disappear.

Look at what your best customers repeatedly use.

Look at what users keep asking for.

But don't automatically turn every request into a feature.

Keep asking:

Does this make the core promise of the app stronger?

Sometimes that means adding a feature.

Sometimes it means deleting three screens.

Sometimes it means getting users to their first result 30 seconds faster.

Maybe the default experience is wrong.

Maybe the output needs to improve.

Maybe one section of onboarding is confusing.

You're trying to improve conversion, revenue, retention or the actual outcome the customer came for.

You're not trying to win an award for the longest feature list.

Once you know what works, scaling becomes almost boring.

One creator consistently produces customers?

Give them more work.

One content format keeps generating downloads?

Make 30 variations.

One ad stays profitable?

Scale it and make more creatives around the same idea.

One audience converts twice as well?

Go deeper.

People imagine scaling as constantly discovering new growth hacks.

A huge part of it is much simpler:

Find something that works and refuse to stop doing it.

## THE WHOLE FORMULA

If I had to compress everything into five steps:

1. Enter a proven market

Find a painful problem people already spend money solving.

You don't need to invent a new market. Multiple competitors making serious money is validation, not necessarily a reason to stay away.

2. Build in 7 days, not 7 months

Study the winners. Understand their decisions. Give Shipper screenshots and references. Build the onboarding, paywall and core loop.

Then keep iterating until it doesn't feel like another AI-generated clone.

3. Treat onboarding as part of marketing

A download isn't a customer.

Users still need to understand the problem, experience enough value to want the result and have a strong enough reason to pay.

4. Test distribution at stupid volume

Find formats that already work and make your own versions.

Don't optimize for views.

Optimize for views → downloads → trials → revenue → retention.

5. Scale what survives the entire funnel

More winning creators.

More versions of winning creatives.

More paid spend behind proven concepts.

Better conversion.

Better retention.

Then repeat.

That's really it.

Don't bookmark this, feel productive for five minutes and then forget about it.

Build something.

title: INTPは、「大切にされるほど」キモく感じる。
body:
好きな人から大切にされるのは、誰だって嬉しいはずです。

でも、INTP（論理学者）の恋愛においては、奇妙なズレが起こります。

相手の好意が強くなりすぎると、なぜか急に相手のことが「気持ち悪い」と感じてしまう。

頻繁に連絡される。「会いたい」と何度も言われる。自分を最優先にしてくれる。

普通なら愛情を感じて喜ぶべき場面なのに、彼らはだんだん距離を取りたくなり、最終的にはスッと心のシャッターを下ろしてしまいます。

一体なぜ、彼らは「大切にされること」から逃げてしまうのでしょうか。

好きだったはずなのに、急に冷める

INTPは、相手に興味を持っている段階では、自分から相手を知ろうとします。

「この人は何を考えているんだろう？」という知的な好奇心が、恋愛感情につながることも多いです。

ところが、相手が自分に夢中になりすぎると、関係性の空気が一変します。

相手を知りたいという純粋な気持ちよりも、「相手の重たい期待に応えなければならない」という感覚が勝ってしまうのです。

すると、あんなに好きだったはずなのに、会うことや連絡を返すことが、急に『こなさなければならない業務』のように感じられてしまいます。

愛情が「嬉しいもの」から「義務」に変わる

ここが、INTPの恋愛が壊れる一番の核心です。

例えば、相手から何度も「好き」と言われる。最初は純粋に嬉しい。

でも、次第に彼らの頭の中ではこんな計算が始まります。

「自分も同じ熱量で返さなければいけないのかな」

「返信が遅いと傷つけてしまうかな」

「今日は一人でいたいと言ったら、嫌われるかな」

すると、ただ愛情を受け取っていただけの関係に、突然『責任や義務』が生まれます。

INTPにとって何より苦しいのは、愛情が重いことではありません。

「大切にされた分だけ、こちらも自分を削って何かを返さなければならない」と無意識にプレッシャーを感じてしまうことなんです。

相手の好意が強くなるほど、逃げ場がなくなる

INTPは、一人で考えたり、好きなことに没頭したりする「一人の時間」を命と同じくらい大切にします。

ところが、相手が自分を最優先にするようになると、その自由が少しずつ奪われていくように感じます。

返信しないと心配される。一人でいたいと言うと寂しがられる。

相手には全く悪気がなく、むしろ好きだからこそ大切にしてくれているのは分かっています。

でもINTPからすると、相手の愛情を受け取るたびに、自分の大切な「自由」を差し出しているような息苦しさを覚えてしまうのです。

だから、相手の好意が「キモく」見えてくる

本来なら、相手の好意と、相手自身の魅力は別のものです。

しかし、好意が強すぎて窮屈さを感じるようになると、相手の行動すべてが違って見えてきます。

以前は嬉しかった「会いたい」が、今は重い。

以前は可愛く感じた嫉妬が、今は面倒くさい。

以前は嬉しかった気遣いが、今は監視されているように感じる。

相手が変わったわけではありません。愛情を受け取るときの、INTP自身の感覚が変わってしまったのです。

この残酷な変化を、INTP本人もうまく説明できずに戸惑い、自己嫌悪に陥ることがあります。

彼らが本当に求めているのは「放置」ではない

誤解してはいけないのは、INTPは愛情を向けられたくないわけではないということです。

むしろ、好きな相手とは深く、確実に繋がりたいと願っています。

ただし、「いつでも一緒にいたい」よりも、「離れていても安心できる関係」を求めているのです。

毎日連絡しなくても、気持ちを疑われない。

一人で過ごしたいと言っても、責められない。

そんな関係であれば、相手の愛情を「義務」ではなく、素直に嬉しいものとして受け取ることができます。

INTPは、大切にされることが嫌いなのではありません。

大切にされることで、自分の自由まで失うのが極端に苦手なだけなのです。

彼らは、愛情が重いから冷めるわけではありません。

「愛情が義務に変わった瞬間」に、冷めてしまうのです。

好きだからといって、すべてを共有したいわけではない。一人の時間があっても、愛情はなくならない。

INTPが心から安心できるのは、離れていても絶対に愛情を疑われない、そんな風通しの良い関係なのかもしれませんね。
