## How Bee keeps your conversations private

Privacy has been part of Bee’s design since the very beginning. Both Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse are built on Bee Private Compute, a security architecture that processes your conversations inside a secure and isolated processing environment where no one, including Amazon, can access your data. Here’s how it works:

- No audio is ever stored. Audio is processed into insights in real time and deleted after processing.

- No one else can access your data unless you choose to share it. Transcripts are encrypted using keys that only your device creates and controls. Transcripts are accessible only to you unless you choose to share them.

- You’re always in control. A single press turns on and off Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse with an LED light to signal the device is on.

- Personalized Alexa access. If you connect Bee to Alexa, your Echo device uses voice ID to recognize your voice and provide your Bee insights to you.

- You decide what to keep. You can delete your transcripts and summaries at any time.

## Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse: Availability and pricing

Bee Frontier is available now for $74.99 in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage at Amazon.com. Bee Eclipse will be available soon, starting at $99.99 in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush.

With the purchase of Bee, all users receive conversation summaries, recaps, and 14-day memory at no additional cost. With a Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited recent conversation summaries; integrations with Amazon.com and Alexa+; integrations with third-party applications; suggested to-dos; daily memories; a personal chat assistant; and conversation templates; and the Bee desktop application. Bee Pro costs $11.99 per month. All new Bee customers get 30 days free of Bee Pro.

*Some Bee features require a Bee Pro subscription. Learn more about Bee.

title: The Sun’s pick for Nevada governor: Aaron Ford
body:
Like most elected leaders, Joe Lombardo has done some good things and failed to do other good things. But in 2022, he had the opportunity as a respected leader in the Republican Party to do one thing: to tell the truth about the 2020 election — that Trump lost fair and square. Instead, he ducked the question.

His abject failure to tell Nevadans the truth about election fraud continues to this day and has significantly contributed to the ongoing distrust in our democratic institutions. Couple that with his shocking overuse of veto power and he displays a disturbing lack of respect for democratic processes.

We elect legislators to craft laws, policy and regulations. They represent our will. Lombardo’s obstruction of their work is the same as thumbing his nose at voters. A few vetoes are fine, but 162 vetoes in just two legislative sessions? Unconscionable. For perspective, former Republican Gov. Brian Sandoval previously held Nevada’s gubernatorial record with 97 vetoes accumulated across four legislative sessions.

Among the legislation Lombardo vetoed were bills to lower the costs of housing and prescription drugs, fund universal free school lunches, prohibit convicted criminals from possessing guns and protect access to in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments. Whatever disagreements inevitably arise between a governor and a Legislature controlled by the opposing party, Lombardo’s extraordinary use of unilateral executive power represents precisely the kind of antidemocratic behavior that Nevadans should reject.

Equally concerning is Lombardo’s continued unwillingness to meaningfully separate himself from Donald Trump and the most extreme elements of the Republican Party.

That matters enormously for a state like Nevada, where the Trump administration’s trade wars, aggressive immigration policies and poorly planned and executed invasion of Iran have contributed to a massive decline in international visitation, sent consumer prices skyrocketing and created uncertainty for Nevada businesses and workers. Visitation from Nevada’s largest international tourism market, Canada, has declined nearly 30% since Trump took office.

We believe the greatest threat to our democracy and our way of life today is the continued sycophancy of the Republican Party to Trump’s narcissistic tendencies. Yet Lombardo continues appearing alongside Trump while offering little meaningful resistance when the president’s actions threaten Nevada’s interests. Nevadans deserve a governor willing to defend this state even when doing so requires breaking with his own party.

Aaron Ford offers an alternative record.

As attorney general, Ford’s office has helped secure more than $1.2 billion in opioid-related recoveries for Nevada, completed the testing of 7,814 previously backlogged sexual-assault kits, prosecuted human traffickers and child predators, and prosecuted Medicaid fraud referrals at twice the national average. He has also fought against Trump’s worst impulses at every turn, filing or joining in more than 40 lawsuits against the Trump administration.

That does not mean Aaron Ford is above criticism. We have serious concerns about whether he will behave differently than his opponent when faced with tough decisions and not simply look for the “safe” or “politically opportune” way out. Courage is not optional in a political environment in which people’s lives and livelihoods are at stake. We encourage Ford, if he is elected, to rise to the occasion, put our concerns to rest and prove he has the character and fortitude to defend working families and put Nevada’s interests first.

Lombardo was given the chance to profile his courage and chose instead to remain silent in the face of Trump’s excesses while Nevadans suffered. He should not be rewarded with a second term.

Instead, we should elect Aaron Ford as the next governor of Nevada.

title: KOSPI Crash and Bitcoin $80K: The AI Chip Selloff Trade Plan
body:
Bitcoin did not crash on a crypto headline yesterday. It dipped to $80,154 while a stock market in Seoul halted trading, and that is a different kind of risk to plan for.

TL;DR: South Korea's KOSPI tripped circuit breakers and closed down about 7.5% as an AI chip selloff met a hot US inflation print, dragging bitcoin to its lowest level since Sept. 20 before a rebound above $82,000. Nearly $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated, altcoins fell harder than bitcoin, and the next catalysts (Waller today, FOMC on Oct. 28, SK Hynix and Samsung earnings) are all macro. The trade is to define your levels now and let orders do the work, not to chase the bounce.

## What Happened: KOSPI Circuit Breakers and a $80K Wick

On Thursday the KOSPI fell as much as 9% intraday, a circuit breaker halted trading after an 8% drop, and the index closed at 5,554, down 7.5% on the day and about 15.5% on the week, its lowest close since April 8, according to Cointelegraph. SK Hynix dropped about 11% and Samsung Electronics about 9.5%. Reports tied the move to hotter-than-expected US inflation and doubts about AI chip spending, though outlets differ on how much weight each factor deserves.

Bitcoin traded down to $80,154 on Bitstamp overnight, its lowest print since Sept. 20, then recovered to roughly $82,200 by the start of the Friday session. Ether sat near $2,440 after dipping close to $2,360 during the move. Two points worth keeping: the $80K area is also where the Oct. 8 low sits near $80,300, and bitcoin held it twice now.

## Why a Korean Stock Crash Reaches Crypto

Crypto is a 24/7 market, so it is often the first liquid venue to react when equity markets close or halt. When Seoul stopped trading, risk had to go somewhere, and leveraged crypto positions were an easy place to cut exposure. That does not mean KOSPI and bitcoin are tightly correlated. CoinDesk linked the two moves but did not quantify a correlation, and it would be a mistake to build a thesis on one day of overlap.

What it does show is a shared driver. The AI trade has been carrying equities, and when financing concerns surfaced (CoreWeave rallied back to close up about 6% after dropping more than 8% intraday on default rumors), semiconductor stocks sold off for a seventh straight session. A market that leans on the same narrative across asset classes breaks together when the narrative cracks.

## The Derivatives Damage: Liquidations and Where the Shorts Are

According to CoinDesk, liquidations jumped to nearly $1 billion over 24 hours from about $136 million the day before, with roughly $200 million in ether longs and $115 million in bitcoin longs wiped. Futures volume rose 61% to about $252 billion while open interest stayed roughly flat near $139.6 billion.

Two details matter for positioning. First, bitcoin open interest rose about 1.6% while price fell, which can signal new short-side money, although open interest alone does not show direction. Second, funding on BTC, ETH and SOL remains positive, so longs are still paying to hold. If price chops sideways, that bleed continues; if it breaks lower, there is more fuel for another flush.

Implied volatility, measured by BTC's BVIV, rose to just above 40% from lows near 34%, still well below the panic readings from earlier this year. This is stress, not capitulation.

## Altcoins Fell Harder: Who Bled and Who Held

Most of the market was red. CoinDesk's memecoin index fell about 4%, Pump.fun dropped 9.4%, Canton fell 7.3%, Optimism 7.0%, Aerodrome 6.4%, Jito 6.2% and Jupiter 6.1%. Only six members of the CD100 finished higher.

The exceptions are instructive. Starknet rose about 11% on a community poll about moving toward quantum resistance, Pyth gained around 3% to 11% depending on the snapshot, and Injective rose on a new institutional validator. Those are idiosyncratic catalysts, not a sign that alts are decoupling. Thin books amplify both directions, which is exactly why altcoin entries punish market orders.

## Levels and Catalysts to Watch This Week

Support and resistance as cited by analysts and exchange reports, not guarantees:

- Support: $80,000 to $80,300 (the double-tested zone), then roughly $79,400 and the $77,000 to $80,000 band if it breaks.

- Resistance: $82,500 to $83,000, then $85,000.

- Ether: about $2,360 was the low of the move; $2,400 is the level to reclaim.

On the calendar: Fed governor Waller speaks at the IMF meetings today, and the market has moved on Fed hike odds since the CPI print (CME FedWatch readings of 47% to 54% were reported for an Oct. 28 hike, depending on the source and time of day). September PPI came in at 6.3% year over year against 5.3% expected, with the monthly gain of 1.3% the largest since March 2022. SK Hynix reports Q3 earnings on Oct. 28 and Samsung on Oct. 29, which lands on the same days as the FOMC decision window. Token unlocks for ARB today and ASTER and CRO tomorrow add supply on top of a nervous tape.

## The Trade Plan: Define It Before the Next Halt

Nothing here is financial advice, and every level below is an illustration of structure, not a recommendation to buy or sell.

1. Decide your invalidation first. If you are long bitcoin above $80K, the stop belongs below the double-tested zone, not at the exact wick.

2. Scale in, do not stab in. Split an entry into two or three limit orders between $80,500 and $82,000 rather than one market buy into resistance.

3. Pair every position with exits. A take-profit near $83,000 to $85,000 and a stop under support turns a view into a plan.

4. Size for gaps. A circuit-breaker day shows moves can skip levels. Smaller size beats a tighter stop.

5. Treat alts as a separate bet. They fell harder and bounce on thinner volume.

The reason to write this down in advance is that these moves happen while you sleep. A halt in Seoul landed in the middle of the night for US traders. Fere AI is built for exactly that gap: you describe the plan in plain English, such as "buy $300 of ETH in two limit orders at $2,380 and $2,330, set a 12% take-profit and a stop-loss at $2,200", and the agent places and manages the orders across supported chains, including TP/SL on tokens no exchange lists. Wallets are non-custodial, so you keep control of the keys.

## The Takeaway

The signal from the last 24 hours is that macro is driving crypto, the AI trade is a shared point of failure, and bitcoin has now defended roughly $80K twice. Do not guess which way the Fed or the chip stocks break. Pick your levels, size small enough to survive a gap, and let orders handle the rest. If you want to set a plan like this up in a couple of sentences, you can start with Fere AI.

title: summer at forus
body:
I had the privilege of spending the past few months interning at @Forus, fka Tandem, one of the fastest growing AI startups in the world, and I wanted to share a bit about my time and learnings.

Forus is building the AI network for medicine: the platform connecting doctors, pharmacies, payers, and biopharma to bring new science to the patients who need it.

The company recently announced a $150M Series C at a $3B from investors including @ThriveCapital , @generalcatalyst, @Accel and @neo

## how i decided to go work at forus

This starts in February 2026. I read this Anthropic blog where they measured verticals/domains in which agents are actually being deployed in

Software engineering, to no one's surprise, was #1. But if you look toward the bottom of the chart, medicine and healthcare was at just 1%.

Healthcare felt like a place where deploying AI could have a very direct positive impact on peoples lives/the world so I was pretty appalled by how few agents were deployed in healthcare.

At the time, I was in conversation with several companies building consumer agents, fintech products, ecommerce products, and computer use agents.

But I decided I wanted to work in AI + healthcare.

So I tried to find what I thought was an impactful place to work. I asked friends for warm intros, talked to people in the space, and eventually came across Forus.

I cold applied and interviewed, chatted with friends and investors familiar with the space about the company, and came away pretty convinced this was the place I wanted to go work at.

One of the things that stood out to me about Forus was how aligned the incentives were between everyone involved.

1. Patients want access to their medication.

2. Doctors want their patients to get their medication.

3. Pharmaceutical companies want patients who have been prescribed their drugs to actually receive them.

That felt different from a lot of other healthtech businesses I had looked at, and was one of the reasons I found the company so compelling.

I was still on the fence for a multitude of reasons [ie. considering working at bigger companies, for the name/branding], but one of my friends recommended I read @eladgil's piece on career decisions.

I found it to be a really helpful framework for thinking through the decision, especially his point around prioritizing the people you work with.

I ended up signing my offer in february and formally joined in april

# engineering at forus

Over the summer, I got to work on a bunch of different problems across our product, data, and infrastructure, including:

- building internal apps for our operations team

- building dev tools for engineers

- working on our core systems for data extraction

- making browser agents go vroom

- automating processes that previously required manual intervention

- reducing repeated lookups/load by adding a cache to our system

- thinking a lot about where agents actually make sense in production systems

What surprised me most was how much business context was required to actually build many of these things.

I spent a lot of the first part of my internship understanding our data models, how they mapped to the real world, and what the downstream effects of my changes would be.

What does it mean to be a "practice"? What's the relevance of a "prescription" or "Rx"? How does a prescriber relate to all of this? If I change something here, what happens somewhere else in the system?

I also did my fair share of stalking Slack to learn everything possible lol :p

Working across so many different problems, with a lot of autonomy, was one of my favourite parts of the internship.

I wrote more about some of the technical work, including how we thought about browser agents and automations, here

# learnings and takeaways

Coming into this experience I had two goals:

1. I wanted to learn more about healthcare and what it actually looks like to build in a vertical

2. I wanted to firsthand see what it was like to be at a fast growing, post PMF company

I achieved both of those and came away with a bunch of learnings, but to really distill it down into a few:

You can actually just ask for things

- I was initially pretty reluctant to ask for help, feedback, or support because I didn't want to bother people or take up their time

- As the internship went on, I realized that everyone at the company was ultimately working toward the same mission and generally wanted to help

- You can ask to sit in on a meeting if you think you belong in the room, ask to work on a different project, ask someone to look at your work, or ask to try something you haven't done before

- The worst that usually happens is someone says no, but I think people underestimate how much opportunity comes from simply asking

- We often leave ourselves stuck in situations we don't like, or miss things we would have learned from, because we're too scared to ask

- I want to be much more intentional about asking for things when I think they would help me learn or do better work

Being able to articulate your thoughts and ideas is just as important as engineering skill

- A lot of good communication is making it easy for someone else to help you make a decision

- This is something I became much more conscious of over the summer

- Being able to explain what you're building, why you're building it, where you're blocked, and what has changed is incredibly important

- When asking for help or feedback, it's much more useful to explain what you've tried, what you think the next step should be, and why

Writing by hand and having brevity is important

- At the start of my internship I produced my fair share of slop docs, like many others at the company

- Midway through the internship we made a rule that all documents produced at the company had to be written by hand

- In sitting down to actually write PRD/TRDs I found I was forced to clarify my thoughts and found gaps in my own thinking more easily

- It's hard, but so valuable, and I want to put a lot more emphasis on improving this skill

- Long on all killer no filler

Having tight feedback loops matters a lot

- PRDs, TRDs, design reviews, code reviews, testing, and keeping people updated can look like process around the work

- I came away realizing that a lot of this is the work- especially as a team and product scale, having good process is what allows people to continue moving quickly

- Good process is about creating tighter feedback loops and making it easier for people to work together

Understanding the business is a much bigger part of engineering than I thought

- The internal tooling surprised me because understanding what should be built, how our workflows integrated with it and the business impacts was much harder than building it out

- I came away realizing how important it is to actually understand the business around the software to make good technical/product decisions

Getting your work critiqued by other people is extremely valuable

- I underestimated this before the internship

- Getting feedback on your ideas, designs, writing, and implementation early is incredibly high leverage

- There were many times where a design review or conversation with another engineer changed how I was thinking about a problem before I spent a bunch of time building the wrong thing

- The value of working around really good engineers isn't just getting to observe them. It's getting to have them look at your work and tell you where you're wrong so being intentional about that is important!

Not everything needs to be agentic

- I came into the summer very excited about making things more agentic and left much more interested in asking where the agent actually needs to be

- Sometimes the right answer isn't having an agent do the work every time

- It might be using an agent to help create something deterministic 

- I also came away with a much greater respect for simple, reliable systems and not glorifying complexity which humans (and agents) often love to do! [Intentional Code - Minimalism in a World of Dogmatic Design - David Whitney - NDC London 2023]

Recruiting is really, really, really hard

- I got to spend a bunch of time in conversations about recruiting, engineering brand, events, and how to convince really good people to come work at a company

- I underestimated how much time and thought goes into building a great team, this is truly one of the, if not the hardest part of building a company

Having a defensible moat for a company is extremely important

- One of the things that originally attracted me to Forus was how aligned the incentives were across stakeholders

- Especially as software gets easier to build, I think distribution and operational problems and being deeply embedded into how customers operate matter a lot

- I’ve come to appreciate that the best businesses have structural reasons to get better as they scale (ex. network effects)

## outside of engineering

I also got to host a bunch of fun events and spend a lot of time in conversations about recruiting, how to build a brand, fundraising, healthcare, and a bunch of other things I previously knew very little about.

More generally, getting to spend a summer in New York surrounded by such amazing people was an incredible experience. Some of my favourite memories from the summer:

- the team surprising me with mango cake on my birthday

- late night white boarding at the office with ishaan and heemy

- yankees games with the team

- lots and lots of mimis froyo and la cabra lattes

I'm incredibly grateful for all the people I got to meet and spend time with this summer.

## thank you

Special thanks to Rohit, Ezra, Anton, @abeinstein and @sahirjaggi for their mentorship and support

A big thank you to @ishaanr4, @alexlerner_, Ally, @mihirarya, Tyler, Liz and the whole team for making this internship such a memorable experience. It was a pleasure working with you. Miss you all :)

title: The Agentic-Web Cheatsheet
body:
Agents are the new browsers. More and more of the visits to your site will come from an AI agent that someone sent to compare, book, buy or file a return on their behalf. Since mid-2025, a dozen new open standards have appeared to teach websites how to deal with that.

They're easy to mix up. They're young, they overlap, several are only drafts, and the press releases make all of them sound finished. So here's the whole map in one place: what each standard does, who's behind it, and how real it actually is today.

The short version: twelve standards, five jobs, and only four of them (UCP, ACP, x402 and Web Bot Auth) carry real production traffic yet. Some help an agent find what a website offers, some let it use the site directly, some prove who the agent is, some let it shop, and some let it pay. The rest are drafts or early experiments.

> This article is a snapshot. The living version, kept up to date and open to contributions, is at ax.guide.

Read it left to right as an agent's visit: find what's offered, use the site, prove who it is, shop, then pay. Green means real traffic today; x402's is real but small.

## 1. ARD: Agentic Resource Discovery

A search engine for agent tools. Today an AI assistant can only use the tools someone wired into it beforehand, like a phone that only runs its pre-installed apps. ARD flips that. A website publishes a small file at /.well-known/ard.json (".well-known" is just the web's agreed folder for files like this, the same idea as robots.txt) listing what it offers: an MCP server, an agent other agents can talk to, an API, a skill. Separate "registries" collect these files and answer plain-language searches. Say your travel agent needs a live-weather tool it has never heard of: it asks a registry, gets a ranked list, checks who published each tool, and connects. A high ranking doesn't mean a tool is trustworthy; the spec keeps relevance and trust separate. Entries can include sample questions a real user would ask, which makes search work better.

Google announced ARD on June 17, 2026. The current version is v0.91, a "Proposal" dated August 26, 2026, from authors at Google and Hugging Face plus R.V. Guha (the creator of RSS and Schema.org). It tells agents to look for ard.json first and treats the older ai-catalog.json address as its predecessor. On July 9, 2026 the two formally split into a publishing format (ai-catalog) and a discovery format (ARD). The file name changed within a few months, so early tutorials already show the old address.

Reality check: early. Hugging Face runs a public registry, but one independent check in June found that none of the named contributor companies served a catalog yet.

## 2. ai-catalog: AI Catalog

Your site's table of contents for AI. It doesn't contain the chapters; it tells you where each one is. MCP servers, AI agents, plugins and datasets each invented their own way to be found, so an assistant would have to know a dozen conventions. AI Catalog replaces that with one JSON list at /.well-known/ai-catalog.json, where each entry says what kind of thing it is and either links to its full description or includes it. A restaurant that works with a booking provider and a jobs provider can list both AI tools, so any assistant that only knows the restaurant's web address can find the booking tool. Catalogs can also point to other catalogs, so a big platform can list many sub-catalogs.

It's developed in a Linux Foundation working repository (started October 2025) with members from the MCP and A2A communities, and published at ai-catalog.io. Even the group's name is inconsistent: ai-catalog.io calls it the "Agent Card Working Group," while Google thanks the "AI Catalog Working Group." Its biggest recent boost: MCP's "Server Cards" proposal points discovery at ai-catalog.json (reported as finalized October 6, 2026, though one implementer still saw it in review). ARD calls ai-catalog its predecessor, but ai-catalog sees itself as a lightweight publishing format that stays separate: it was split off, not retired.

Reality check: early, with experimental catalogs at GitHub, Buildkite and Hugging Face. The fix is easy: serve the same file at both ai-catalog.json and ard.json.

## 3. NLWeb

Your website's own shop assistant, one who answers from your stock list rather than making things up. Most websites already describe their content in structured ways (Schema.org tags, RSS feeds), yet you can still only search them with keywords. NLWeb indexes that structured data and adds an "ask" endpoint: type "vegetarian recipes under 30 minutes without nuts" and get answers drawn only from that site. Every NLWeb site is also an MCP server, so AI agents can ask the same questions through a standard plug. Cloudflare offers a one-click "NLWeb Website" option that crawls your site and sets up an /ask page for people and an /mcp endpoint for agents.

Microsoft introduced it at its Build conference on May 19, 2025; R.V. Guha conceived it. The code is open source and the current spec is v0.55. A W3C community group launched in October 2025 but still has no chairs, 15 participants and no published reports, and community groups aren't a standards track, so NLWeb is not a W3C standard. Launch partners included Allrecipes, Eventbrite, Tripadvisor, O'Reilly and Shopify. A security bug that let attackers read server files was reported and fixed in mid-2025. It complements ARD and ai-catalog (which can list an NLWeb endpoint) and differs from WebMCP, which works inside the browser page.

Reality check: early. Nobody publishes a deployment count, partly because NLWeb has no fixed address to crawl.

## 4. WebMCP

A labeled menu of actions for the agent in your browser. More and more AI assistants work inside your browser, clicking and typing on the page for you. Today they mostly do it by looking: reading the page's code or a screenshot, guessing which box is "departure date," and hoping the "Book" button didn't move in last week's redesign. WebMCP lets the site say it plainly. A page registers "tools" in JavaScript (document.modelContext.registerTool()) with a name, a plain-English description, the fields it expects and the function that does the work, or tags an existing form with two attributes, toolname and tooldescription. On a hair-salon site, the agent stops hunting for the calendar widget and calls book_appointment with a date, time and service. It all happens in your own tab and signed-in session, so you can watch and step in.

Microsoft and Google proposed it together in August 2025; the W3C's Web Machine Learning community group took it up that September, with editors from both companies. The current text is a draft dated October 9, 2026 that says plainly it is "not a W3C Standard." Chrome has been testing it in a time-limited "origin trial" (Chrome 149–156) since May 2026; on September 28 Google asked to extend the trial to Chrome 162 because feedback is still changing the API, so there's no ship date. Edge runs its own trial (since Edge 150, through March 30, 2027) and calls it "ready for testing." ChatGPT's desktop browser calls these "site tools" automatically, and Shopify puts WebMCP tools on every standard storefront, including a checkout tool that only completes after the buyer confirms. Safari's team opposes it and Firefox is neutral. Its neighbours: MCP servers serve agents that never load your page, and computer-use agents that read the screen remain the fallback. A related layer, MCP Apps (not one of the twelve), goes the other way: it lets an MCP server ship interactive UI into the agent's chat. One caveat: a page's tool descriptions are text the AI reads, so a malicious site can try to trick the agent, and Chrome says the defence is the agent's job.

Reality check: early use with two big real-world users, ChatGPT's desktop browser and Shopify, while Chrome and Edge are still in trials.

## 5. Web Bot Auth

A tamper-proof ID badge for bots, instead of a name tag anyone could write. Today websites identify bots by a label (the "user agent") that anyone can fake, or by IP address, which breaks easily. With Web Bot Auth, the company running the bot publishes a public key at a well-known address and signs every request with the matching private key, using an existing IETF standard for signing web requests (RFC 9421). The website, or its CDN such as Cloudflare, checks the signature and knows for certain "this really is OpenAI's agent" before deciding to let it in, block it or charge it. A news site can let a verified shopping agent through while stopping an anonymous scraper wearing the same label.

Cloudflare proposed it in May 2025. On September 1, 2026 the IETF's webbotauth working group adopted it as an official working-group draft, written by authors from Cloudflare and Google; it's the group's only adopted document. It's still a draft, not an RFC: adoption isn't approval. Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and Mastercard's Agent Pay build on it, adding a tag that says whether the agent is browsing or buying, and observers report OpenAI, Cloudflare and DuckDuckGo signing requests today. It answers which agent is visiting, not whom it represents; that's Poppy's and OAuth's job. The next revision is expected to change how the key directory is referenced, so early implementations may need updates.

Reality check: in production. A draft, but a real one.

## 6. Personal Agent Protocol (Poppy)

A valet key for your personal agent. It lets the agent act for you at a company, with only the permissions you gave it, without opening the boot or the glovebox. Right now an AI agent acting for you has two bad options: pretend to be you in a browser, or not get in at all. Poppy gives the company a file at /.well-known/poppy.json that says how agents can start a session, how you sign in, and which web pages, APIs and company agent are available. Sign-in uses OAuth, the familiar "Sign in with…" approval screen: you approve on the company's own page, on another device with a code, or (if the company allows it) the agent signs in for you. Permissions are simple scopes like "read" and "write," plus custom ones such as "manage saved addresses." You also get a different anonymous ID at each company, so companies can't match you with each other. In the launch demo, Meta's Muse agent found Rocket Mortgage's agent and, with the user's permission, completed a mortgage pre-approval.

Sierra (led by Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor) and Meta announced it on October 6, 2026, with Genesys, Instinct, Rocket, Shopify, Stripe and Walmart as partners, then published Draft 0.1 on October 9 with 35 design partners (reported to include OpenAI, Visa, Mastercard and PayPal). The spec warns that any part can change, even in ways that break compatibility, and lists payments as not yet covered. A reference implementation is promised within about a month. It reuses OAuth, OpenAPI and MCP rather than replacing them, sits next to Web Bot Auth (which proves the bot's identity), and leaves shopping to UCP/ACP and payment consent to AP2.

Reality check: a draft first published October 9, 2026. Impressive partners, but no company is publicly known to serve a working poppy.json yet.

## 7. auth.md

A sign-up page written for robots. When your agent needs a service you've never used, it hits a wall built to keep bots out: an email, a password, a CAPTCHA, a confirmation link. So it stops and asks you to make an account and paste back a key. auth.md replaces the wall with instructions at yourapp.com/auth.md. Ask a coding agent to add web scraping to your app, and it calls the scraping service, gets "401: who are you?" plus a pointer to the service's login details and auth.md file, then signs you up one of three ways: vouched for, where the company running the agent signs a short-lived pass saying "this is a verified user" and registration finishes on its own; by email, where you type a 6-digit code on the service's own page; or anonymously, where the agent starts with limited access and you "claim" the account later. Either way, it ends with a normal, short-lived, revocable OAuth token tied to you.

WorkOS, an identity company, published it as an open, MIT-licensed spec on May 21, 2026 and shipped six versions in three weeks, reaching v0.6.0 on June 10. It isn't with any standards body; WorkOS's own recap calls it "a spec, not an IETF-ratified standard." It's built from existing parts: OAuth's login-discovery files, and a vouching token ("ID-JAG") that is itself a draft in the IETF's OAuth working group. WorkOS lists 15 adopters, and implementations vary a lot: Neon lets an agent spin up a temporary database the person claims within 72 hours; Cloudinary does the same with a temporary media cloud claimable within 24 hours; monday.com has the agent solve a captcha and then creates the account; Firecrawl only accepts identities vouched for by WorkOS; Cloudflare and Resend said "not yet" at last check. Several follow the idea more than the exact spec. MCP's latest spec (2026-07-28) recommends identifying the app with Client ID Metadata Documents, while auth.md adds on whose behalf; Poppy signs in existing customers, auth.md signs up new ones.

Reality check: early use, and growing. The fully hands-free "vouched for" path needs the big agent makers to issue those passes, and none (Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor) has announced it yet.

## 8. UCP: Universal Commerce Protocol

A universal power socket for shopping. Any assistant plugs into any store without a custom adapter. UCP defines the common steps of buying (catalog, cart, checkout, order) and carries them over ordinary web APIs or the plugs agents already use (MCP, A2A). A store describes what it supports at /.well-known/ucp. Ask Google's AI Mode for waterproof hiking boots under $150, and it compares several shops and checks out right in the chat, while the retailer stays the "merchant of record," the legal seller who handles returns and customer data.

Google launched it with Shopify on January 11, 2026, co-developed with Etsy, Wayfair, Target and Walmart. A Governing Council has Google and Shopify as permanent members, and Stripe joined on April 28; a technical council added Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Salesforce and Stripe in April, and industry councils for food, lodging and payments followed over the summer. A council seat isn't a storefront: Amazon being at the table doesn't mean Amazon sells through UCP. The current release, v2026-08-25, added support for more industries and stronger card security. Its rival is ACP, AP2 plugs in for payment consent, and Poppy may overlap on sign-in.

Reality check: in production, and the most real of the twelve: an independent checker counts more than 15,000 verified storefronts, mostly through Shopify. One catch: the August release made 17 breaking changes, so "supports UCP" doesn't tell you which version.

## 9. ACP: Agentic Commerce Protocol

A catalogue mailed straight to your personal shopper, with an optional order form attached. ACP started as the plumbing for buying inside ChatGPT: a merchant shares a product feed and checkout endpoints, and payment travels as a one-time token tied to one merchant and one amount, so the assistant never holds your card number. The original idea: ask ChatGPT for a ceramic mug, see an Etsy seller's listing, and tap to buy without leaving the chat. Today its main job is discovery: merchants push feeds and promotions so ChatGPT shows accurate, current products, prices and comparisons.

OpenAI and Stripe launched it on September 29, 2025, alongside "Instant Checkout" in ChatGPT. The spec is still labeled beta; its latest stable version is dated April 17, 2026. On March 24, 2026 OpenAI said it was expanding ACP to support product discovery, naming Target, Sephora, Nordstrom, Lowe's, Best Buy, The Home Depot and Wayfair as integrated, while checkout moved back to the merchant's side. Its rival is UCP (Stripe sits in both camps), and payment rails like AP2, MPP and x402 can sit underneath.

Reality check: in production for discovery. The headline feature that launched ACP, buying inside ChatGPT, is exactly the part that was scaled back.

## 10. AP2: Agent Payments Protocol

A signed, notarized shopping list with a spending limit the bank can check before paying. When an agent pays, the bank and merchant need answers to "did a real person agree to this?" and "who's liable if it goes wrong?" AP2 answers with mandates, tamper-proof signed records of your instructions. An intent mandate captures what you asked for ("concert tickets, under $200, this week"); a cart mandate locks the exact items and price; a payment mandate tells the card network an agent was involved. Version 0.2 adds "Human Not Present" purchases: you pre-sign the rules, and the agent buys later when conditions are met, say when tickets go on sale at 3 a.m. It works with cards, bank transfers and stablecoins. AP2 authorizes payments; it doesn't process them.

Google announced it on September 16, 2025 with more than 60 organizations, including American Express, Coinbase, Mastercard, PayPal and Salesforce. On April 28, 2026 Google released v0.2 and handed AP2 to the FIDO Alliance (the group behind passkeys), which formed working groups chaired by members from Google, OpenAI, CVS Health, Visa and Mastercard. Mastercard's Verifiable Intent, a similar auditable record of what a user approved, co-developed with Google, went to FIDO at the same time. FIDO's work is only months old, so v0.2 isn't yet a FIDO-approved standard.

Reality check: early. Real use is mostly inside other protocols, like the AP2 extension in UCP's latest release; consumer-facing AP2 checkout is still limited.

## 11. MPP: Machine Payments Protocol

A turnstile that takes a tap of your card. No account, no membership; pay and walk through. Paying for an online service usually means signing up, getting a key and setting up billing, which an autonomous agent can't easily do. MPP uses the web's long-unused "402 Payment Required" code: the server replies "this costs 2 cents, here's how to pay," the client pays, and the server returns the result plus a receipt. It supports one-off charges, subscriptions and streaming pay-as-you-go "sessions," with stablecoins on Stripe's Tempo blockchain or ordinary cards through Stripe. Picture a research agent paying a fraction of a cent per article from a paywalled archive and settling the total when it finishes.

Stripe and Tempo launched it on March 18, 2026, the same day Tempo's payments blockchain went live. Its core spec is an IETF Internet-Draft (draft-httpauth-payment-01, September 9, 2026), but an individual one: the IETF lists it as having no formal standing, and no working group has taken it on. The ecosystem is growing (Circle drafted a USDC payment method), and MPP now accepts x402's simplest payment flow from the same toolkit, so the two are more compatible than competing.

Reality check: early use, live on Tempo. Unlike x402, no neutral foundation owns it; it's written and maintained by two companies with a commercial stake.

## 12. x402

A parking meter on every web page. Drop in a few cents and the gate opens; no account needed. The internet never had a built-in way to charge tiny amounts, so content is either free with ads or behind subscriptions. With x402, a server answers "402: pay $0.01 to this address," the client attaches a signed stablecoin payment (usually USDC), and a "facilitator" settles it on a blockchain in seconds, for fees of a fraction of a cent that card networks can't match. Picture an agent paying a weather API a cent per lookup, or a crawler paying a publisher per page instead of being blocked.

Coinbase created it, and version 2 shipped on December 11, 2025. The Linux Foundation announced an x402 Foundation on April 2, 2026 and made it operational on July 14 with 40 members; the 17 premier members include AWS, Google, Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Stripe, Shopify, Cloudflare, Coinbase and Circle, the broadest coalition of any agent-payment standard. Its neighbours: MPP (which now accepts x402 flows), AP2 (which can settle through it), and Web Bot Auth (Cloudflare pairs them for pay-per-crawl).

Reality check: in production, but small. Cumulative counts range from about 100 million to more than 200 million transactions, but CoinDesk (March 11, 2026) found about $28,000 a day of real payments, averaging about 20 cents, with roughly half judged artificial. Cloudflare's "billion 402 responses a day" counts payment requests, not payments. Count dollars, not transactions.

## What's real, what's hype

Three patterns jump out once you see all twelve side by side.

Platforms move faster than standards bodies. The standards with real traffic are the ones a big platform switched on: Shopify accounts for most of UCP's 15,000+ verified storefronts and puts WebMCP tools on every standard storefront; Visa and Mastercard build on Web Bot Auth; OpenAI pipes ACP feeds into ChatGPT. The drafts with the most impressive partner lists are often the ones with no known deployments.

Partner lists aren't adoption, and transaction counts aren't commerce. A design-partner list isn't a deployment list, and 100 million+ cumulative transactions can sit next to about $28,000 a day of real payments. When you read an announcement, ask two questions: who has actually turned it on, and how much real money moves through it?

The plumbing is still settling. File names are shifting (ai-catalog and ARD split into publishing and discovery formats within months), APIs are still changing mid-trial, and the headline commerce experiment of the past year, buying inside ChatGPT, was scaled back. Build in a way that survives that: one source of truth, published in more than one place.

## Side by side

All twelve side by side, in the same order as the map.

Then comes the money: shopping and paying, where most of the live traffic is.

## The cheat sheet: when to use which

- You offer APIs, MCP servers or agents and want to be found → ARD and ai-catalog: serve the same file at both ard.json and ai-catalog.json

- Agents use your site inside people's browsers → WebMCP on your key flows, keeping the normal page

- You have lots of structured content people and agents want to query → NLWeb

- Your bot visits other sites, or you need to verify bots on yours → Web Bot Auth

- You want agents to create accounts on your service without a sign-up form → auth.md

- Customers' own agents should sign in and act on their accounts → Poppy (track it; Draft 0.1 is from October 9, 2026)

- You sell goods and want any AI assistant to browse, cart and check out → UCP

- You want your products shown in ChatGPT → ACP

- An agent pays and you need proof a person approved those exact terms → AP2

- Agents pay per call or by the minute, with cards or stablecoins → MPP

- You charge per API request in stablecoins, with no accounts → x402

The pairs people mix up: ARD vs ai-catalog (discovery vs. publishing; serve both), UCP vs ACP (any assistant vs. ChatGPT), MPP vs x402 (cards and stablecoins via Stripe vs. stablecoin payments per request under a neutral foundation), and Web Bot Auth vs auth.md vs Poppy (which bot is this / sign up a new user / act for an existing customer).

## The point

Agents are becoming the web's main users. These twelve standards are the plumbing for an agent's whole visit: find what's on offer, act on the site, prove who it is, shop, and pay. What matters in the end is whether the agent actually finishes the job.

## Contribute

> These standards change monthly, so this list will too. ax.guide is the open-source version: every standard is a file, and if something here is wrong or missing, open a pull request.

Status as of October 11, 2026.

title: WISE Token: Understanding the Ethereum-Based DeFi Ecosystem
body:
Web3 is full of projects promising high yields, innovative tokenomics, and long-term value. But smart users know that the headline numbers are only part of the story.

> The more important questions are straightforward: What does the protocol actually do? Where do its rewards come from? What happens when market conditions change? And which risks remain even when the underlying mechanics are transparent?

WISE Token is an Ethereum-based DeFi ecosystem built around WISE/ETH liquidity, time-locked staking, referral incentives, and newer real-world-asset (RWA) yield products.

Its official documentation describes a system designed around self-custody and on-chain mechanics, allowing users to interact with smart contracts rather than relying entirely on a centralized intermediary.

This breakdown examines the project’s stated design, its potential strengths, and the risks users should understand before participating.

The goal isn’t to promote blind optimism or dismiss the project without examination. It’s to understand what WISE offers, distinguish documented mechanisms from unverified outcomes, and encourage independent research.

What is wise token : $WISE is an ERC-20 token deployed on Ethereum mainnet on October 8, 2020, according to the project’s historical materials.

Its original design brought together three major components:

- A WISE/ETH liquidity pool created using ETH raised during the launch.

- A staking mechanism that allows users to lock WISE for selected periods.

- Referral and Critical Mass share mechanics designed to incentivize community participation.

The ecosystem has since expanded its positioning to include revenue-linked buy-and-burn mechanisms and RWA-oriented yield strategies.

The project’s official materials describe WISE as a hardened ETH reserve with an emphasis on what it calls “Provable Neutrality.”

The important distinction is that WISE isn’t simply a staking token. Its design combines liquidity infrastructure, token issuance, staking incentives, and mechanisms intended to connect ecosystem activity with WISE’s circulating supply.

Whether those mechanisms deliver their intended economic outcomes is a separate question that requires evidence.

What Problem Is WISE Trying to Solve?

One of the central ideas behind decentralized finance is reducing reliance on traditional intermediaries.

In conventional financial products, users may depend on institutions to hold assets, process transactions, calculate returns, and manage withdrawals. Centralized crypto platforms can introduce similar dependencies.

WISE positions itself as an alternative built around direct interaction with smart contracts.

Instead of relying solely on a company’s promises, users can examine the relevant on-chain transactions and contract logic. This approach can improve transparency, although it doesn’t eliminate every form of trust or risk.

The project also addresses a common concern in token launches: liquidity that can be withdrawn by whoever controls the liquidity-provider tokens.

According to WISE’s documentation, all ETH raised during the launch was used to establish the WISE/ETH liquidity pool, and the associated liquidity-provider (LP) tokens were burned.

The intended benefit is to prevent a team or treasury from withdrawing that original pool’s liquidity through control of those LP tokens.

This is a meaningful design distinction, but it should be understood precisely.

Burned LP tokens do not guarantee a stable token price, unlimited liquidity, or a guaranteed exit value. They address a specific liquidity-withdrawal risk, not every possible market risk.

How WISE Staking Works

Staking is one of the core components of the original WISE ecosystem.

Users lock WISE tokens for a selected duration. According to the project’s staking documentation and original Teal Paper, staking rewards are funded through WISE inflation.

The documented allocation is:

- 75% of annual inflation: allocated to stakers.

- 25% of annual inflation: allocated to referral incentives.

The original design describes a 4% annual inflation schedule, with 3% allocated to stakers and 1% to qualified referral participants.

Users should consult the current contract rules and documentation before relying on these historical parameters.

Several mechanics deserve attention.

Time-locked participation

Users select a staking duration. Longer stakes are described as having greater earning power, making the length of the commitment an important consideration.

Early-exit penalties

Ending a stake early can trigger penalties. Users should understand the applicable formula before committing tokens, especially if they might need access to those funds unexpectedly.

Reduced immediate circulation

When WISE is locked in a stake, those tokens aren’t immediately available for ordinary trading during the lock period. This changes the amount of WISE available for immediate circulation, although the broader supply dynamics also depend on issuance and other activity.

Rewards paid in WISE

WISE staking rewards are denominated in WISE, rather than automatically providing a fixed return in dollars, ETH, or stablecoins.

That distinction matters.

A user may receive more WISE tokens while the market price of WISE falls. In that situation, the fiat value of the rewards could decline even if the staking contract operates exactly as designed.

Token-denominated APY is not the same as a guaranteed fiat return.

Anyone evaluating staking should consider token-price volatility, inflation, lock duration, and potential exit penalties together.

The WISE/ETH Liquidity Reserve

WISE’s original liquidity design is one of its most discussed features.

Project materials state that 55,900 ETH was paired with WISE at launch and that the resulting Uniswap LP tokens were burned.

The stated objective was to create an initial WISE/ETH pool that couldn’t be withdrawn by a party controlling the original LP tokens.

Why does this matter?

In some token launches, a team or treasury retains control of the liquidity-provider tokens. If that party removes liquidity, traders may find it harder to sell their holdings without substantial price impact.

Burning LP tokens can remove that particular withdrawal option for the burned position.

However, there is an important distinction between locked liquidity and guaranteed value.

A WISE/ETH pool contains both assets, and its composition changes as users trade. Selling pressure can move the price, and large trades can experience significant slippage.

The existence of an ETH-backed pool does not mean every WISE holder can redeem tokens for ETH at a fixed price.

The liquidity design should therefore be evaluated as a mechanism for reducing one category of counterparty risk—not as insurance against losses.

Understanding WISE Buy-and-Burn Mechanics

The broader WISE ecosystem introduces another mechanism: using platform revenue to buy and burn WISE.

According to the Wise One documentation, 90% of platform revenue is directed toward buying and burning WISE. The project’s materials also describe revenue from Wise RWA Nodes being used for this purpose.

The mechanism is intended to connect ecosystem activity with token supply.

The basic process is:

1. The ecosystem generates revenue from its products.

2. A portion of that revenue is allocated to purchasing WISE.

3. The purchased tokens are burned.

4. The burn permanently removes those tokens from circulation, assuming the mechanism operates as documented.

Reducing circulating supply can contribute to scarcity, all else being equal. But scarcity alone doesn’t determine market price.

Demand, liquidity, new issuance, broader crypto-market conditions, and actual revenue levels all matter.

For that reason, the most useful questions aren’t simply whether a buy-and-burn mechanism exists.

- Which products generate the revenue?

- How much revenue has actually been collected?

- How much has been spent buying WISE?

- Are the resulting purchases and burns verifiable on-chain?

- How do the burn amounts compare with ongoing token issuance?

- Are the reported figures current and independently reproducible?

These questions help distinguish the existence of a mechanism from its actual economic impact.

WISE and Real-World-Asset Yield Strategies

WISE has also expanded into real-world-asset-oriented yield products.

Project communications describe Wise RWA Yield Strategies as a way to connect on-chain capital with real-world assets, with USDC or USDT deposits referenced in its announcements.

The project’s broader materials also discuss sectors such as internet infrastructure and energy, including products referred to as Wise Telecom Nodes or AirNodes.

These products introduce a different risk profile from native WISE staking.

Native staking versus RWA yield

WISE staking is described as operating through a defined token-inflation schedule. Its rewards are denominated in WISE.

RWA strategies, by contrast, may depend on real-world businesses, physical infrastructure, operators, contractual arrangements, counterparties, and the ability of an underlying activity to generate revenue.

That means an RWA product can involve risks that aren’t fully visible on-chain.

For example, a smart contract might execute correctly while an off-chain operator experiences financial difficulties. Blockchain transparency alone cannot guarantee the performance of the underlying business.

Before depositing into any RWA strategy, users should investigate:

- Underlying assets: What specific assets or business activities support the yield?

- Revenue generation: Where does the income actually originate?

- Operators and counterparties: Who manages the underlying activity, and what responsibilities do they have?

- Custody: Who controls the deposited assets, and how are they held?

- Withdrawals: Can users withdraw immediately, or are there lockups or other restrictions?

- Audits: Which contracts have been audited, and does the audit cover the particular strategy?

- Failure scenarios: What happens if revenue declines, an operator defaults, or withdrawals exceed available liquidity?

The existence of an RWA product does not, by itself, establish the quality or sustainability of its yield.


What Makes WISE Different?

WISE isn’t the only DeFi project to use staking, token burns, or liquidity locks.

Its distinguishing feature is the way these mechanisms were combined in its original token design and subsequently incorporated into a broader ecosystem.

Area

WISE’s stated approach

Initial liquidity :

Launch liquidity was established through a WISE/ETH pool, with the original LP tokens reportedly burned.

Staking :

Users can lock WISE for selected periods under the documented staking rules.

Reward allocation :

The original tokenomics allocate inflation between stakers and referral incentives.

Buy-and-burn :

Official documentation describes using 90% of platform revenue to purchase and burn WISE.

Community incentives :

The original system includes referral and Critical Mass share mechanics.

Self-custody : 

Users interact with Ethereum contracts through their wallets, subject to the permissions and design of the contracts involved.

RWA products: 

Newer ecosystem offerings aim to connect on-chain deposits with real-world-asset-oriented strategies.

The key point isn’t that these features eliminate risk.

It’s that they create specific mechanisms users can investigate.

The quality of that investigation depends on whether contract permissions, transactions, financial flows, and product terms can be verified independently.

What Still Requires Careful Verification?

Some claims are best treated as mechanisms or targets to investigate, rather than proof of an outcome.

“Provable Neutrality”

The project uses the phrase “Provable Neutrality” in its official positioning.

Users should examine what this means at the contract level. Relevant questions include whether there are owner privileges, upgrade controls, emergency-pause functions, minting permissions, or other administrative capabilities.

A claim about neutrality should be assessed against the actual code and governance arrangements.

Revenue-backed burns : 

The documentation describes directing 90% of platform revenue toward buying and burning WISE.

To assess the mechanism’s economic significance, users need current evidence of revenue, purchase transactions, burn transactions, and ongoing issuance.

A stated percentage doesn’t tell the whole story without the underlying amounts.

RWA yield claims : 

Project communications have referenced an advertised yield of up to 22% APY for RWA-related products.

An advertised maximum isn’t necessarily the average yield, the yield currently available to every user, or a guaranteed return.

It also doesn’t establish the risk-adjusted outcome after fees, losses, counterparty problems, or withdrawal restrictions.

Users should verify the current product terms and underlying yield source before depositing funds.

The “ETH floor” interpretation

The original WISE/ETH liquidity design is a feature worth examining.

However, describing a pool as an “ETH floor” can create the mistaken impression that WISE has a guaranteed minimum redemption price.

A liquidity pool does not provide that guarantee. Its composition and exchange price change with trading activity.

The Main Risks to Understand :

No meaningful DeFi assessment is complete without examining downside scenarios.

Smart-contract risk : 

Smart contracts can contain vulnerabilities, and an audit cannot guarantee that all bugs have been found.

Users should confirm which contracts have been audited, whether the deployed code matches the reviewed version, and whether newer products rely on additional contracts.

Market risk : 

WISE is a crypto asset whose market price can rise or fall substantially.

Because staking rewards are denominated in WISE, token-price declines can reduce the fiat value of both the original position and the rewards earned.

Liquidity and slippage risk : 

Burning LP tokens can reduce the risk of an administrator withdrawing the original liquidity position.

It doesn’t guarantee stable market depth, low slippage, or the ability to sell large amounts at an expected price.

Early-unstaking penalties : 

The WISE staking documentation describes penalties for early termination, with costs linked to stake duration.

Users should understand the precise rules and calculate potential exit costs before locking tokens.

RWA counterparty risk : 

Real-world-asset strategies depend on off-chain operations and counterparties.

Revenue can change, operators can experience problems, and contractual or legal disputes can affect the underlying activity. A functioning blockchain transaction cannot eliminate these risks.

Regulatory and tax risk :

Crypto assets, staking, referral systems, and RWA products may be subject to different regulations and tax treatments depending on the user’s jurisdiction.

Users should understand the rules that apply to them.

Impersonation and name confusion : 

WISE Token is distinct from Wise, the international payments company.

Because the names are similar, users should be careful with search results, social-media accounts, unsolicited messages, and links that claim to offer official services.

Always verify the exact project and contract before connecting a wallet.

A Practical Due-Diligence Checklist: 

Before staking WISE or depositing into any related product, consider these steps.

1. Start with official documentation.

Use the project’s official website and documentation to locate the relevant product information. Independently verify contract addresses rather than trusting links from unsolicited messages.

2. Review contract permissions.

Check ownership, upgradeability, pause functions, minting privileges, and other administrative controls where applicable.

3. Verify the liquidity design.

Examine the original LP-token burn transactions and current pool composition. Don’t confuse permanently burned LP tokens with a guaranteed token price.

4. Understand the staking formula.

Review the reward calculation, lock duration, inflation assumptions, and early-exit penalties.

5. Trace buy-and-burn transactions.

Look for verifiable purchases and burns, and compare their scale with ongoing token issuance.

6. Investigate the RWA product separately.

Identify the underlying activity, revenue source, operator, custody arrangements, withdrawal terms, and audit coverage.

7. Evaluate the downside before the upside.

Consider what happens if the token price declines, yields change, liquidity becomes thinner, or an underlying business underperforms.

8. Manage exposure carefully.

Avoid committing money needed for essential expenses or near-term obligations. Never assume that advertised yields will continue or that you can exit a position at the price you expect.

 A Balanced View of WISE : 

WISE has a documented history on Ethereum, an original liquidity-burn design, a time-based staking system, and a broader ecosystem that describes revenue-linked buy-and-burn mechanisms.

Those are concrete areas for users to examine.

At the same time, the existence of these mechanisms doesn’t prove that the token will appreciate, that revenue will remain consistent, or that newer RWA products will sustain their advertised yields.

The original staking model and the newer RWA offerings also shouldn’t be treated as having identical risk profiles.

The former is built around token-denominated rewards under documented issuance rules. The latter can introduce off-chain operational and counterparty dependencies that require separate investigation.

The most useful way to evaluate WISE is to focus on evidence:

- Are the contract mechanics consistent with the documentation?

- Can the claimed liquidity and burns be verified?

- Are revenue figures available and meaningful?

- Do the risks match the user’s understanding and tolerance?

- Are the specific products being evaluated covered by relevant audits and transparent terms?

These questions lead to a more informed assessment than hype or blanket dismissal.

Final Thoughts

The real value of studying a DeFi project isn’t finding a promise that sounds attractive. It’s understanding the mechanics behind that promise and identifying what could go wrong.

WISE combines Ethereum-based staking, a permanently locked original WISE/ETH liquidity position, referral incentives, and newer revenue-linked and RWA-oriented mechanisms.

Its design provides several specific features worth investigating, but none removes the risks associated with crypto markets, smart contracts, liquidity, or real-world business activity

Official Resources

WISE website: https://www.wisetoken.com/

Wise One documentation: https://docs.wise.one/

WISE Teal Paper: https://www.wisetoken.net/teal/

Additional references from the original research draft:

- The WISE Ecosystem — https://docs.wise.one/

- WISE Token — https://docs.wise.one/wise-token

- Staking WISE — https://docs.wise.one/wise-token/staking_wise

title: Food Is Part of the Café Concept
body:
A coffee house can offer more than drinks without losing its focus.

Café Barbera’s menu includes Italian inspired panini, Mediterranean salads, croissant breakfasts, cheeses, fresh vegetables and pastries. These choices give the café a wider culinary identity while keeping coffee at the centre of the experience.

What stands out to me is the range of occasions this creates. A guest might visit for a light breakfast, choose a panino later in the day or enjoy a coffee alongside a pastry.

The menu is therefore not just a list of additional products. It helps define how the café fits into everyday routines.

For @Barbera_1870, this connection between coffee and food reflects the broader character of a traditional Italian coffee house.

I appreciate that approach because a strong café concept should make sense as a whole. The food, drinks and setting should feel like parts of the same idea rather than unrelated additions.

#ItalianCoffee can be the starting point, while the menu helps complete the visit.

A thoughtful #Coffee experience does not have to be complicated. It simply needs a clear identity and a reason for people to return.

That is a practical way to understand the role of food within the café. #Espresso #CoffeeBreak #GoodMorning

title: Gemini 4 Argonに最初に任せる10の仕事
body:
最上位モデル、何に使っていますか。

Googleの最上位モデル「Gemini 4 Argon（アルゴン）」が使えるようになりました。日本時間の10月14日（米国時間13日）から、Geminiアプリの有料プランで選べます。ただ、選べるようになっても、何を頼めばいいかで手が止まる人は多いと思います。

僕もそうでした。最初の1時間は、いつもの質問を投げて「速いな」で終わっていました。

そこで、Gemini 4 Argonでやる価値がある仕事を、10個に絞って順位をつけました。Googleが公表している評価の数字と、僕が実際に投げてみた結果から並べています。

この記事で得られるもの

- Gemini 4 Argonに、どの仕事から任せるかの順番

- 動画の仕事を、Gemini 4 ArgonとGemini Omniで分けるやり方

- 10個それぞれの、コピーして使える頼む文

- 使える量の上限で困らないための、軽いモデルとの分け方

内容は、2026年10月15日にGoogleの公式の発表とヘルプで確認したものです。

## 第1章 始める前に知っておく3つのこと

順位に入る前に、3つだけ押さえておきます。ここを飛ばすと、第1位の仕事で早速つまずきます。

1つ目は、使える人です。Geminiアプリで使えるのは、有料のGoogle AI ProとUltraの契約者です。無料のプランでは選べません。

モデルを選ぶ一覧にGemini 4 Argonが無いときは、アプリを最新にしてから開き直してください。

2つ目は、動画を作るのはGemini 4 Argonではない、という点です。Geminiアプリで動画を作っているのは、Gemini Omniという動画を作るモデルです。ヘルプでも「Googleの最新のAI動画生成モデル」として紹介されています。

なので、この記事の動画の仕事は2つに分けています。動画を「読む」仕事と、動画の「台本と頼む文を書く」仕事はGemini 4 Argonです。映像そのものを作るのはGemini Omniです。

| 仕事 | 担当 |
|---|---|
| 録画を見て、内容を手順書や要点にする | Gemini 4 Argon |
| 作りたい動画の台本と絵コンテを書く | Gemini 4 Argon |
| 映像を作る（音つきの短い動画） | Gemini Omni |
| 出てきた映像を見て、直す点を言葉にする | Gemini 4 Argon |

3つ目は、使える量の上限です。Geminiアプリの使用量は、5時間ごとにリセットされます。それとは別に、1週間ごとの上限もあります。

ヘルプには、モデルが高度で考える量が多いほど、使用量を多く消費すると書かれています。最上位のGemini 4 Argonで、天気や言葉の意味まで聞くのはもったいない使い方です。

AIを使い始めた頃、僕はAPIの仕組みを分かっていませんでした。APIは、ほかのアプリからAIを呼び出す窓口で、使った分だけ請求されます。気づいたら、10万円単位の請求が来ていました。定額のアプリなら請求は来ませんが、上限に当たれば仕事が止まるのは同じです。

だから僕は、軽い質問はFlash、重い仕事だけGemini 4 Argon、と最初に決めました。Flashに回しているのは、次のような仕事です。

- 言葉の意味や、ちょっとした調べもの

- 1〜2行の返信の下書き

- 短い文章の誤字の確認

- 表の並べ替えや、単純な書き換え

どれも、答えが1回で決まる仕事です。逆に、材料が多い仕事・長い仕事・判断の根拠を見せてほしい仕事は、Gemini 4 Argonに回します。下の10個は、その「重い仕事」の候補です。

順位は、2つの点で決めました。Googleの公表した評価でGemini 4 Argonがはっきり強いか。そして、会社員が毎週やる仕事に近いか、です。

一番高いモデルは、一番重い仕事にだけ使うから元が取れるんです。

## 第1位 会議や研修の録画を読ませて、手順書にする

1位は、録画を読ませる仕事です。動画の理解は、Gemini 4 Argonの数字が一番分かりやすく強いところです。

Google DeepMindが公表した表では、長い動画を理解する評価（LVBench）で91.7%でした。比べている他社のモデルは87.5%・83.7%・79.7%で、Gemini 4 Argonが1位です。

会社には、見返されない録画がたくさんあります。研修の録画、操作の説明の録画、会議の録画です。1時間の録画を見返すのは、誰にとっても重い仕事です。

僕はセミナーの録画を1本、Gemini 4 Argonに渡してみました。頼んだのは「受講した人が、明日1人で操作できる手順書」です。

返ってきたのは、画面の操作ごとに番号の付いた手順と、講師が口で補足した注意点の一覧でした。正直、ここまで「口で言っただけのこと」を拾うとは思っていませんでした。

僕はAIが元から得意だったわけではありません。できないなりに、工夫を重ねて少しずつ覚えてきました。録画を「見る」のをやめて「読ませる」のも、その工夫の1つです。

- Before：1時間の録画を見返して手順書にするのに、約2時間

- After：録画を渡して手順書の下書きを受け取り、見直すだけで約30分

週に1本ある人なら、1年で約78時間が浮きます。毎日8時間働く人の、10日分くらいです。

つまずきやすいのは、動画の長さです。アップロードできる長さの上限は、公式のページでは確かめられませんでした。長い録画は、話題ごとに分けて渡すほうが確実です。

## 第2位 動画の台本と絵コンテを書かせて、Gemini Omniに渡す

2位は、動画を作る前の仕事です。ここが、今回いちばん伝えたかった使い方です。

Gemini Omniは、音つきの動画を作れます。Geminiの動画づくりの紹介ページには、10秒の動画を作れると書かれています。ただ、短い動画ほど、頼む文の1行でできあがりが大きく変わります。

「店の紹介動画を作って」とだけ頼むと、どこの店でも使えそうな映像が出てきます。何を映し、何秒で、どんな音を入れるかを決めていないからです。

そこで、台本と絵コンテ（場面ごとに、何をどう映すかを書いた表）をGemini 4 Argonに書かせます。そのうえで、Gemini Omniに渡す頼む文まで作らせます。Googleは、Gemini 4 Argonは書き方の指示に、これまでのどのGeminiよりも従うと説明しています。細かい条件を守らせたい台本と、相性がいい仕事です。

僕はセミナーの告知の動画で試しました。Gemini 4 Argonに10秒の台本を書かせて、その頼む文をGemini Omniに貼っただけです。一発で「告知に使える」と思える映像が出てきました。

Xの投稿で、僕は「どの形が反応するか」を数えきれないほど試してきました。時間帯も、図解かスレッドかも、全部です。その遠回りから分かったのは、作る前に台本があるかないかで、試す回数がまるで変わることです。

最初から台本を作ればよかったやん...と、何度思ったか分かりません。

- Before：思いつきの頼む文で動画を作り直し、5回目でやっと使える1本

- After：台本と頼む文を先に作り、1〜2回目で使える1本

できた映像に不満があれば、その映像をGemini 4 Argonに見せて「どこを直すか」を言葉にさせます。ここで第1位の「動画を読む」力がもう一度効きます。

動画を、月に1本も作らない人は、この使い方は飛ばしてかまいません。そのぶん、第1位の「読む」ほうに時間を使ったほうが元が取れます。

動画を作ってくれるのはOmniでも、何を作るかを決めるのはArgonの仕事なんです。

## 第3位 バラバラの資料から、提案資料を作る

3位は、Googleが発表の中で見せていた使い方です。

発表には、Gemini 4 Argonが提案資料を作る例が出てきます。整理されていない資料のフォルダから、お客様向けの資料に整える例です。そのときに、自分で作ったスキル（決まった仕事のやり方を覚えさせたもの）を使っています。

提案資料づくりで一番時間がかかるのは、書くことではありません。メール・議事録・見積もりのメモなど、散らばった材料を集めて並べる作業です。

僕は、ある案件の打ち合わせメモ3本と、お客様からのメール、前回の見積もりを渡しました。頼んだのは、10枚の提案資料の構成と、各ページに書く文章です。

返ってきた構成には、各ページに「どの資料のどこから取ったか」が付いていました。材料にない数字は【要確認】のまま残っていて、勝手に埋めていませんでした。

保険の営業と人事の現場で、僕は数千人の人と向き合ってきました。そこで身についたのは、相手の困りごとから話し始める癖です。

提案資料も同じです。材料にないことを書いた資料は、相手の期待をずらします。

- Before：材料を集めて構成を考えるまでに、半日

- After：材料を渡して構成と文章の下書きを受け取り、1時間で見直し

この使い方は、できあがった資料をそのまま送らないことが前提です。根拠の（ ）を見ながら、数字だけは必ず自分の目で確かめてください。

## 第4位 何十本もの議事録から、決まったことと宿題の一覧を作る

4位は、長い資料をまとめて読ませる仕事です。

Google DeepMindの表では、とても長い資料を読み取る評価（GraphWalks）で84.2%でした。2位は71.8%で、12ポイント以上の差があります。

議事録は、1本ずつなら読めます。困るのは、3か月分を通して「結局、何が決まって、誰の宿題が残っているか」を知りたいときです。

僕は、ある定例会議の議事録を12回分まとめて渡しました。頼んだのは、決まったことの一覧と、終わっていない宿題の一覧です。

返ってきた一覧では、途中で変わった決定が「何回目に、何から何へ変わったか」まで並んでいました。僕が忘れていた宿題も、2つ出てきました。

見なかったことにしたかったです。

何年か前の僕は、毎日3〜4時間の残業をしていました。自分の何かをする時間が、まったく取れない生活です。あの頃の自分に一番渡したいのが、この使い方です。

- Before：3か月分の議事録を読み直して宿題を洗い出すのに、約3時間

- After：まとめて渡して一覧を受け取り、元の議事録で確かめて約40分

議事録が別々のファイルでも、まとめて渡せば読めます。ただ、議事録の書き方がばらばらだと、担当が空欄になりやすいです。次の会議から書き方をそろえるきっかけにもなります。

## 第5位 契約書や規程の、気になる条文を表にする

5位は、法律の文書を読む仕事です。

法律の仕事の評価（Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark）の結果です。Google DeepMindの表では19.6%でした。2位は6.7%で、約3倍です。数字そのものは低く見えますが、それだけ難しい評価です。

先に、線を引いておきます。契約が有効か、どちらが不利かを決めるのは、弁護士などの専門家の仕事です。Gemini 4 Argonに任せるのは、その手前の「どこを読めばいいか」を探す作業です。

僕は、取引先から届いた業務委託の契約書のひな形で試しました。頼んだのは、支払い・解約・責任の範囲・秘密の扱いの4つについて、条文の番号と中身を表にすることです。

返ってきた表には、「解約の申し出は何日前か」「損害の上限があるか」が条文の番号つきで並びました。読むべき場所が3か所に絞れたので、そこだけ時間をかけて読めました。

保険の営業をしていた頃、僕はお客様への説明が足りず、保険金が支払われないかもしれない事態を起こしかけました。最終的には支払われましたが、それ以来「伝わったつもり」が一番怖いと思っています。

契約書も同じです。読んだつもりの1行が、あとで一番困る1行になります。

- Before：契約書を頭から読んで、気になる所に線を引くのに約1時間

- After：表で読む場所を絞ってから読み、約20分

社外に送る契約や、金額が大きい契約は、この表を持って専門家に相談してください。表があるだけで、相談の時間はかなり短くなります。

## 第6位 決算書や数字の資料から、要点と質問を作る

6位は、数字の資料を読む仕事です。

金融の調べものの評価（Vals Finance Agent v2）の結果です。Google DeepMindの表では65.4%でした。2位は58.9%です。Geminiアプリのリリースノートでも、得意なこととして複雑な財務の報告書の分析が挙げられています。

ここで言う数字の資料は、決算書だけではありません。取引先の決算の公告、自社の月次の売上表、補助金の申請書の予算の表なども入ります。

僕は、ある会社が公開している決算の資料をGemini 4 Argonに渡しました。頼んだのは、前の年から大きく動いた数字を5つと、その理由として資料に書かれていることです。

返ってきた5つには、どのページの表から取ったかが付いていました。理由が資料に書かれていない数字は、「理由の記載なし」と正直に書いてありました。

人事の仕事をしていた頃、僕は採用1人あたりの費用を3.5万円まで下げたことがあります。業界の相場の10分の1から20分の1です。数字を下げるには、まず数字がなぜ動いたかを知る必要がありました。決算書を読むときも、見るのは同じところです。

- Before：資料を読んで、打ち合わせの質問を考えるのに約1時間半

- After：要点と質問の下書きを受け取り、数字を確かめて約30分

計算した数字には、必ず「計算」と付けさせてください。資料の数字とAIが計算した数字が混ざると、あとで見分けられなくなります。

## 第7位 前置きなしのメールを書かせて、書き方を保存する

7位は、毎日の文章の仕事です。地味ですが、使う回数は一番多くなります。

Googleは、Gemini 4 Argonの書き方の変化を説明しています。ぼかした言い方が少なく直接答えること、ありきたりな決まり文句を使わないことなどです。

Geminiに「メールを書いて」と頼むと、前置きと「お役に立てれば幸いです」がついてくる。そんな経験がある人は多いと思います。この癖が減ったのは、毎日のメールではかなり効きます。

僕は、日程の調整・お礼・お断りの3通を書かせてみました。前のモデルと同じ頼み方で、出てきた文から消した文字の数を比べています。前のモデルでは毎回2〜3行を消していましたが、Gemini 4 Argonでは消したのは1通あたり1行程度でした。

Xのフォロワーが8,000人から1年半まったく伸びなかった時期があります。原因は、自分が話したいことだけを話していたことでした。読む人の側に立って書くようにしたら、一気に伸びました。メールも同じで、相手が最初の1行で用件が分かる文が一番伝わります。

- Before：AIの下書きから前置きと決まり文句を消して、1通5分

- After：用件から始まる下書きを少し直して、1通2分

1日10通の人なら、毎日30分、1か月で約10時間浮く計算です。

メールを1日に数通しか書かない人は、ここは急がなくて大丈夫です。逆に、お客様とのやりとりが多い人ほど、差が大きく出ます。

この頼む文は、次の第8位で保存しておくと、毎回貼る手間がなくなります。

## 第8位 自分の仕事のやり方を、スキルにする

8位は、Gemini 4 Argonに自分のやり方を覚えさせる仕事です。

スキルは、何度も使う仕事のやり方を保存しておく機能です。第3位で紹介したGoogleの例でも、提案資料を作るときにスキルを使っていました。同じ日のリリースノートでは、「カスタマイズ」も発表されています。左のメニューから、答え方と、ふだん使うアプリとのつながりを1か所で設定できる機能です。スキルの追加も、同じ発表で案内されています。

スキルにするのは、毎週同じ頼み方をしている仕事です。週報・議事録の形・お客様への報告の形などが向いています。

僕は、第4位の議事録の頼み方をスキルにしました。会議のあとに、メモを貼って「議事録」と頼むだけで、決まった3つの表が返ってきます。毎回、頼む文を探して貼る手間が消えました。

僕は一度、パソコンの初期化で、作業の環境をまるごと失ったことがあります。それまで作ってきた設定と、AIへの指示のまとまりが全部消えました。泣きそうでした...というか、ちょっと泣きました。あのとき思ったのは、頭の中ややり方を「外に書いて残す」ことの大切さです。

スキルも同じです。自分の頭の中にしかない仕事のやり方は、書いて保存した瞬間から、Gemini 4 Argonが毎回守る決まりになります。

- Before：毎回、前に使った頼む文を探して貼る

- After：スキルを呼ぶだけで、いつもの形の答えが返ってくる

画面の名前は、日本語の画面と英語の画面で違うことがあります。左のメニューの「カスタマイズ」から開くと、スキルの置き場所も見つけやすいです。

## 第9位 「タスク」に切り替えて、席を外している間に進めてもらう

9位は、Gemini 4 Argonに長い作業を任せる使い方です。

今回の発表では、チャットから「タスク」に切り替えて、Gemini 4 Argonに作業を任せられると紹介されました。タスクに切り替えると、パソコンの前にいない間も、Geminiが作業を進めます。ヘルプには、Gemini 4 Argonはチャットとタスクの両方で使えると書かれています。

Googleは、Gemini 4 Argonが状況を分かりやすく伝え、使う人を置き去りにしないとも説明しています。任せっぱなしの不安が、少し減ります。

なお、タスクはヘルプで、欧州経済領域・スイス・英国・ナイジェリアでは使えないとされています。日本は、この中に入っていません。

僕は、来週のセミナーで話す3つの話題について、公式の発表を集める作業をタスクで頼みました。頼んでから昼食をとり、戻ってくると、話題ごとの要点と出典のページの一覧ができていました。

ここは脅しを入れておきます。任せる作業が長いほど、途中で間違えたときの影響も大きくなります。Googleは、メールやWebページに隠された悪い命令に強くしたと説明していますが、0%ではありません。

ただし、社内向けの調べものや下書きから始めるなら、心配しすぎなくて大丈夫です。お客様への送信や支払いを任せる段階になってから、確かめる場面を決めれば間に合います。

- Before：昼休みを削って、調べものを続ける

- After：昼休みの前にタスクで頼み、戻ってから確かめる

最後の「送信・予約・支払いはしない」の1行は、必ず入れてください。タスクで任せる範囲を、自分で決めておくための1行です。

## 第10位 写真や画面の画像、手書きのメモを読ませて表にする

10位は、画像を読ませる仕事です。

Googleはモデルの説明書（モデルカード）を公開しています。そこには、Gemini 4 Argonが文章のほかに画像・音声・動画を受け取れると書かれています。第1位の動画と同じで、「見て、整理する」仕事が得意です。

会社には、表にしたいのに画像になっているものが多くあります。ホワイトボードの写真、手書きのメモ、他のシステムの画面の画像、紙のチラシなどです。

僕は、打ち合わせのあとに撮ったホワイトボードの写真を渡しました。矢印でつながった図と、走り書きのやることが混ざった写真です。頼んだのは、やることの表と、図の関係を文章にすることです。

返ってきた表は、矢印の向きを読んで「誰から誰に渡す作業か」まで書き分けていました。読めなかった字は【判読不可】と書いてあって、ごまかしていませんでした。

AIが得意ではなかった頃の僕なら、写真を横に置いて1マスずつ打ち直していたはずです。できないなりの工夫は、こういう地味な所から始まります。

- Before：写真を見ながら、表に打ち直して約20分

- After：写真を渡して表を受け取り、読めなかった所だけ直して約5分

写真は、なるべく正面から、影が入らないように撮ってください。斜めの写真は、読める字の数が目に見えて減ります。

ここまでの10個は、全部やる必要はありません。毎週やっている仕事に一番近い1つから始めれば十分なんです。

## 衝撃的な話です

最上位のモデルを選んでいる人の多くが、その力の9割を「ちょっとした質問」に使って眠らせています！

Gemini 4 Argonが強いのは、長い動画、長い資料、法律と数字、そして長い作業です。逆に言えば、短い質問だけでは、Flashとの差は見えにくいと僕は感じています。

僕も、最初の1時間は「速いな」で終わっていました。重い仕事を1つ渡した瞬間に、やっと使い方が分かりました。AIが元から得意だったわけではない僕でも、順番さえ決めれば使えるようになります。

今日やることは、3つだけです。

1. Geminiアプリのモデルの一覧で、Gemini 4 Argonがあるか確かめる

2. 10個の中から、毎週やっている仕事に一番近いものを1つ選ぶ

3. その頼む文に、手元の録画や資料を1つ付けて投げる

最初の1つが動いたら、その頼む文をスキルにして残してください。そこから先は、毎週あなたの時間が戻ってきます！
